p: The rescuer of the mountains.
s: Some dogs earn a reputation. The Saint Bernard earned a hospice. High in the Swiss Alps, on a pass where storms arrive without warning, monks kept these dogs from the 1600s. Travelers vanished in the snow there. The dogs went out and found them.

By most tellings, they had gifts no human had. They seemed to sense avalanches before they fell. They tracked a buried scent through deep snow. They lay beside a frozen traveler and shared the warmth of a body the size of a small sofa. Then one dog ran back for help.

Barry became the legend. Over twelve years of service in the early 1800s, he is credited with saving about forty lives. He still stands in a museum in Bern. The hospice has kept a dog named Barry ever since.
The famous brandy barrel is a myth. A painter added it to a collar in 1820, and the world believed him. The real rescues needed no help from a cask.

Today the breed is a family dog. It is patient, calm, and enormous. It drools, it leans, and it will try to sit on your lap. It still believes anyone nearby might need rescuing. Usually the rescue is a hug.
Nobody asked these dogs to be heroes. They were asked to be steady. In storm or in calm, the Saint Bernard arrives the same way, slow and certain, as if the mountain were never in doubt.
rc: An alpine rescuer turned family companion (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for the Great St. Bernard Pass, where a hospice was founded in the 11th century by Bernard of Menthon.
Notable Saint Bernards
Barry, the Alpine rescue legend. Beethoven, the slobbering film star of 1992. Cujo, the title dog of Stephen King’s 1981 novel.
Good to Know
Drools and sheds. Overheats easily. Giant breeds often live shorter lives, so choose a breeder who screens hips, elbows, and heart.
Coats & Colors
A smooth or rough coat in red with white markings, or brindle with white. A dark mask and a long, heavy tail.
By the Numbers
Up to 180 pounds. About 2,000 lives credited to hospice dogs over roughly two centuries. Recognized by the AKC in 1885.
d: The hospice sits at 8,100 feet. A warm fire was the rescue.
Legend says one dog lay beside the traveler, one fetched the monks.
That black nose can smell a traveler buried under deep snow.
A Saint Bernard shakes off snow like a wet blanket. Stand back.
The dog at the window is not bored. It is on duty.
The brandy barrel? A painter invented it in 1820. Ask your friends.
Every pup believes it is small, then climbs into your lap.
lw: The leash hangs by the door, and the snow is waiting.

A Saint Bernard’s whole history rests on one question. Who needs help today? The dog asks it of every stranger and every tired person on the path. Often the answer is you. Then the door opens, and the mountain waits, ready to roam.

p: The silent guardian of the snow country.
s: Some dogs love you loudly. The Akita does it quietly. It will not bark for attention or beg for it or announce its devotion. It will simply be there, watching you with calm dark eyes, certain that you already know.

The breed comes from the snowy north of Japan, in the mountains around Akita Prefecture. Hunters there used large dogs to track game as big as bear. A dog like that had to be strong, silent, and steady. The Akita was all three.
Japan came to treasure the breed. The Akita was named a national monument in 1931. Families still give small Akita statues to newborns and the sick, as a wish for health and long life.

Then came Hachiko. Every day in the 1920s, an Akita in Tokyo walked to Shibuya Station to meet his owner’s train. When the professor died, Hachiko kept coming. For about nine years he waited. Today his statue stands outside that station.
Helen Keller is credited with bringing the first Akita to America, in 1937. Soldiers returning from Japan after the war brought more. Americans fell for the breed the same way Japan had.
The Akita is not for everyone. It is large, willful, and reserved with strangers. But to the people it chooses, it gives the long, steady kind of loyalty that never needs words.
rc: A silent guardian from northern Japan (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Akita Prefecture in northern Japan. The prefecture’s name means autumn field.
Notable Akitas
Hachiko, who waited at Shibuya Station for about nine years. Kamikaze-go, the gift to Helen Keller in 1937.
Good to Know
Quiet but strong willed. Reserved with strangers and often with other dogs. Sheds heavily twice a year. Early training matters.
Coats & Colors
A thick double coat in red, white, pinto, or brindle. A plush tail curls over the back.
By the Numbers
Up to 130 pounds. Hachiko waited about nine years. Recognized by the AKC in 1972.
d: The Akita watches the snow fall and approves of the silence.
Akita means autumn field. The breed comes from that Japanese prefecture.
Hachiko met the Shibuya train for nine years after his owner died.
Loyalty is quiet work. The Akita never once explains itself.
Hunters used these dogs on bear. Now they guard the sofa.
Akita colors range from red and white to brindle. All are correct.
A sleeping Akita wraps its tail over its nose like a scarf.
lw: The garden gate is open, and the snow is fresh.

An Akita never rushes out. It pauses on the step, weighs the morning, and decides you are worth walking with. It asks for nothing and gives everything. The gate swings wide, and the garden waits, ready to roam.

p: A lifeguard disguised as a bear.
s: The Newfoundland looks like a bear and acts like a nanny. Huge, dark, and slow to anger, it has spent centuries pulling people out of cold water. It does this without being asked, then looks surprised to be thanked.

The breed comes from the island of Newfoundland, off Canada’s Atlantic coast. Fishermen there needed a dog that could haul nets, drag carts, and work in freezing surf. They got a swimmer with webbed feet, a coat that sheds water, and a heart as large as its paws.

Rescue became its calling. Stories of Newfoundlands saving swimmers and sailors run through two centuries of sea history. Some are legend and many are true. Even today the breed trains for water rescue, and it passes the test by wanting to.

The breed also walks through history and books. Lord Byron adored his Newfoundland, Boatswain, and gave him a monument and a famous epitaph. Lewis and Clark took a Newfoundland named Seaman across the continent. Peter Pan’s nursemaid, Nana, was one too.
At home, the Newfoundland is a gentle giant. It is patient with children, calm with strangers, and fond of leaning on whatever it loves. It also drools, so keep a towel nearby.
Perhaps that is the secret. A dog this strong has nothing to prove. It is simply ready, always, to be the safest thing in the room.
rc: A gentle giant from the Atlantic coast (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for the island of Newfoundland, off Canada’s east coast, where fishermen bred it as a working dog.
Notable Newfoundlands
Seaman, who crossed the continent with Lewis and Clark. Boatswain, Lord Byron’s beloved companion. Nana, the nursemaid of Peter Pan.
Good to Know
Drools and sheds. Needs brushing several times a week. Overheats in summer. Giant breeds often live shorter lives, so choose a breeder who screens heart and hips.
Coats & Colors
A thick, water-resistant double coat in black, brown, gray, or black and white. The broad tail works as a rudder.
By the Numbers
Up to 150 pounds. Webbed feet on every paw. A coat that sheds water like a raincoat.
d: A Newfoundland lies in the doorway like a warm rug.
Webbed feet and an oily coat make this dog built for water.
Seaman crossed the continent with Lewis and Clark in 1804.
That shake can soak a dock, a porch, and a bystander.
Strength this size is only worth having if it is gentle.
Lord Byron gave his Newfoundland, Boatswain, a monument and an epitaph.
The pup learns to be gentle by leaning on the giant.
lw: The cabin door is open, and the lake is still.

A Newfoundland waits for you on the step. It is not impatient. It is simply certain that someone, somewhere, might need rescuing. Today that someone is you. The door swings wide, and the shore waits, ready to roam.

p: An ancient aristocrat in a snow-white coat.
s: The Maltese weighs less than a loaf of bread and carries itself like a duchess. It has no job and wants none. Its work is to sit beside you, shining, and make the room feel more expensive.

This is one of the oldest toy breeds in the world. Ancient Greeks wrote of small, silky dogs from the island of Malta, and Roman ladies are said to have carried them like jewelry. Some think the name comes from an old word for harbor, a place where small dogs came ashore.

Through the centuries the Maltese stayed the same. The long white coat. The black button nose. The dark, steady eyes. Kings and merchants valued them. So did anyone who has ever wanted something soft and loyal in the lap.

That coat is the dog’s glory and its chore. It hangs straight and silky to the floor, with no fluffy undercoat to speak of. It asks for daily brushing, a firm hand with the comb, and a gentle one with the tear stains. Many owners choose a short trim and a sweater.
Do not mistake it for fragile. A Maltese is quick, playful, and a little bossy. It will bark at a snowflake and win the argument. It simply believes that a small dog can hold a large opinion.
And it loves, completely. Pick one up and it settles into your arms as if that was always the plan. It makes one person feel chosen, which is the oldest gift a dog can give.
rc: An ancient companion in a snow-white coat (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Malta, the Mediterranean island tied to the breed since ancient times. Some think the name comes from an old word for harbor.
Notable Maltese
Maf, Marilyn Monroe’s Maltese, a gift from Frank Sinatra. The Roman noblewomen said to have carried them in their sleeves.
Good to Know
Tiny but bold. Needs daily brushing or a short trim. Tear stains need regular wiping. Small bones, so handle gently and keep jumps low.
Coats & Colors
A long, silky single coat in pure white, with light tan or lemon allowed. The tail curves over the back.
By the Numbers
Under seven pounds. A coat that can grow to the floor. Recognized by the AKC in 1888.
d: This blanket belongs to the Maltese. Visitors are welcome to admire it.
Maltese dogs appear in ancient Greek art, over two thousand years ago.
A full-grown Maltese weighs under seven pounds. Smaller than most cats.
Elegance is mostly confidence. The Maltese has never doubted it.
Marilyn Monroe’s Maltese, Maf, was a gift from Frank Sinatra.
Roman women reportedly carried Maltese in their sleeves. Warm, portable, adored.
Two Maltese on a chaise form a small, fluffy committee.
lw: The sweater is on, and the snow is waiting.

A Maltese does not need a long trail. It needs a short one, taken with you, and taken seriously. It trots ahead, checks the world, and trots back to report. The door opens, the leash waits, and the whole small kingdom is ready to roam.

p: The gentle giant who believes he is a lapdog.
s: No dog enters a room like the Great Dane. It arrives. Heads turn. The coffee table retreats. Then this giant lowers itself onto a sofa meant for two and asks for a blanket.

The name is a misunderstanding. The breed is German, not Danish. Hunters there bred big dogs to chase wild boar through the forest. By most tellings, a French naturalist saw the dogs in Denmark and called them grand danois, and the name stuck.
Germany came to love its dog. In 1876 it named the Great Dane a national breed. Admirers have long called it the Apollo of dogs.
Size is the headline. A Great Dane named Zeus stood 44 inches at the shoulder and earned a Guinness record. On his hind legs he stood over seven feet.
Everything else is gentleness. A Great Dane is patient with children, polite with strangers, and certain it is a lap dog. It will lean on you, sigh, and hand you its whole weight as a compliment.
The price of such a heart is a short visit. Giants tend to live only seven to ten years. Great Dane owners know it, and love harder anyway.
rc: The Apollo of dogs (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Not Danish at all. The name is credited to a French naturalist who called the breed grand danois.
Notable Great Danes
Zeus, a record-holder at 44 inches. Scooby-Doo, the Mystery Machine’s mascot. Marmaduke, the comic strip star.
Good to Know
Needs space and a sturdy bed. Prone to bloat, so ask your vet about feeding. Giants often live shorter lives, so choose a breeder who screens heart and hips.
Coats & Colors
A short, smooth coat in fawn, brindle, blue, black, harlequin, or mantle. A long tail tapers to a point.
By the Numbers
Up to 175 pounds. Males stand at least 30 inches. Recognized by the AKC in 1887.
d: The sofa was built for two people. The Dane volunteered.
The Great Dane is German, not Danish. The name was a mistake.
A hundred pounds of dog, and not one ornament was harmed.
Real strength is quiet. The Dane watches the snow fall and waits.
Zeus stood 44 inches tall and set a Guinness world record.
Scooby-Doo is a Great Dane. So is Marmaduke. Ask your friends.
When a Great Dane sleeps, the whole house seems to exhale.
lw: The lanterns are lit, and the steps are dusted with snow.
A Great Dane waits at the door like a guard of honor. It lowers its head to let you clip the leash, then matches its long stride to yours. The door opens, and the winter waits, ready to roam.

p: Adventure always sounds like a good idea.
s: Some dogs ask where you are going. The Siberian Husky has already decided. Eyes blue as glacier ice, tail curled, grin wide, it leans into the cold wind and waits for you to catch up.

The breed comes from northeastern Siberia, where the Chukchi people raised dogs to pull sleds across hundreds of miles of ice. They needed dogs that could run all day on little food. Endurance mattered more than speed, and the Husky has plenty of both.

In 1925 that endurance saved a town. Diphtheria was spreading in Nome, Alaska, and the medicine was 674 miles away. Teams of sled dogs relayed the serum through blizzards in about five and a half days. Togo ran the longest and hardest leg. Balto led the final team into town.
The look is as famous as the history. A thick double coat shrugs off winter. A tail curls like a plume. Those eyes may be blue, brown, or one of each, and every pair seems to be plotting something.
A Husky does not obey so much as negotiate. It sings instead of barking, digs under fences, and treats a closed gate as an opening offer. It needs miles of exercise and plenty of patience from you.
Give a Husky a job, a trail, and a cold morning, and it will give you everything. Joy, mostly. The kind that runs ahead and looks back to make sure you are coming.
rc: The endurance athlete of the north (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Siberia, where the Chukchi people raised the breed. Husky was an old nickname for hardy northern sled dogs.
Notable Huskies
Togo, who ran the longest leg of the 1925 serum run. Balto, who led the final team into Nome. Both are honored with statues in New York City.
Good to Know
Sheds heavily and needs hours of exercise. Digs, howls, and escapes fences. Not a dog for a quiet life or a short walk.
Coats & Colors
A dense double coat in every shade from black to pure white. Masks and markings vary. A plume tail curls over the back.
By the Numbers
Males weigh up to 60 pounds. The 1925 serum run covered about 674 miles in about five and a half days. Recognized by the AKC in 1930.
d: The Husky curls its tail over its nose. Nature’s built-in scarf.
Huskies were bred to run all day on little fuel.
Huskies howl, yodel, and talk back. Barking is for amateurs.
In 1925, sled dog teams relayed medicine 674 miles to Nome.
Curiosity is a kind of courage. A Husky tests the snowman.
Husky eyes can be blue, brown, or one of each. Ask around.
A pile of Husky puppies is a warm engine of joy.
lw: Breath hangs in the air, and the leash hangs by the door.

A Husky will not wait politely, but it will wait. It stands on the step, bright-eyed, sure that the best trail is the one just ahead. It asks only that you come along. The door opens, the snow glitters, and the whole white world is ready to roam.

p: Strength wrapped in kindness.
s: The Bernese Mountain Dog looks like a teddy bear dressed for a formal dinner. Black coat, rust trim, white shirtfront. Then it grins, and the formality ends.

The breed comes from the farms around Bern, Switzerland. Dairy farmers there needed a dog that could guard the yard, drive the cows, and pull a cart of milk and cheese down the mountain. It had to be strong and steady, and kind enough to trust around children.

By the late 1800s the breed had nearly vanished as other dogs and machines took over farm work. Then a few Swiss admirers, including the geologist Albert Heim, set out to save it. Bernese were shown in Bern in 1904, and the revival took hold.
That rescue is why we have them. Today the Bernese is a family dog first. It loves children, shrugs off weather, and believes any gathering would be improved by leaning against someone.
The coat is the signature. Jet black, rich rust, and clean white, with a white blaze on the face and a smudge of rust above each eye. It sheds in great clouds, so keep a lint roller handy.
The heart is the signature too, and it comes with a cost. Bernese often live only seven to ten years. Owners will tell you every one of those years is worth it.
rc: A farm dog with a formal coat and a soft heart (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for the Swiss canton of Bern. Its Swiss name, Berner Sennenhund, means Bernese dairyman’s dog.
Notable Bernese
The Dürrbächler, farm dogs named for the village of Dürrbach, where the breed first drew notice. Albert Heim, the geologist who helped save it.
Good to Know
Sheds heavily and overheats easily. Needs company and a daily walk. Prone to cancer and joint problems, so choose a breeder who screens carefully.
Coats & Colors
A long, silky coat in jet black with rich rust and white markings. The tail hangs low with a gentle curve.
By the Numbers
Males up to 115 pounds. Reportedly able to pull a loaded cart of 1,000 pounds. Recognized by the AKC in 1937.
d: A Bernese lies by the fire, a warm rug with opinions.
Bernese once pulled milk carts down Swiss mountain roads.
A Bernese can reportedly pull a thousand pounds. It prefers games.
Steady beats fast. The Bernese has been proving it for centuries.
Bernese means from Bern, Switzerland. The dog is a local celebrity.
By 1900 the breed was nearly gone. Swiss admirers saved it.
The pup leans against the big dog and falls asleep.
lw: The chalet door is open, and the snow is settling.

A Bernese does not tug at the leash. It leans toward the day, calm and cheerful, and waits for you to join it. It has always walked beside people, from the farm to the mountain pass. The door swings wide, and the Alps wait, ready to roam.

p: A general’s confidence in a teacup of fluff.
s: The Pomeranian is the size of a teapot and has the confidence of a general. It marches into any room, fluffs itself to full height, and expects applause.

The surprise is its ancestry. The Pomeranian descends from large Spitz dogs of Pomerania, a Baltic region of Europe, that herded sheep and pulled sleds. Those dogs weighed up to thirty pounds. Over generations, breeders shrank them to fit in a lap.

Royalty did the rest. Queen Charlotte brought Pomeranians to Britain in the 1700s. Queen Victoria fell for the breed in 1888, when she acquired a small one in Florence, and she bred them smaller still. Fashion followed the Queen.
Fame found small dogs in odd places. Two of the three dogs that survived the Titanic were Pomeranians.

The attitude has never shrunk. A Pomeranian barks at mail carriers, nods at snowflakes, and guards the sofa from anything larger than a cushion. The fluff is real. Under the double coat, the dog is mostly confidence.
Brush it often and handle it gently. In return you get a loyal shadow who thinks you are the most important person in the house, and is usually right.
rc: A fox-faced fluffball with a general’s confidence (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Pomerania, the Baltic region now split between Poland and Germany.
Notable Pomeranians
Marco, the Pomeranian Queen Victoria brought home from Florence in 1888. Two Pomeranians that survived the sinking of the Titanic.
Good to Know
Barks readily and needs early training. Daily brushing keeps the double coat tidy. Small bones, so handle gently. Dental care matters.
Coats & Colors
A thick double coat, most often orange, but also red, cream, black, sable, and more. A plume tail lies over the back.
By the Numbers
Three to seven pounds, though its ancestors reached thirty. Recognized by the AKC in 1900.
d: The Pomeranian has claimed the best chair. No appeal is possible.
Pomeranians descend from Spitz dogs many times their size.
Queen Victoria fell for Pomeranians in 1888 and bred them smaller.
Confidence is not a matter of size. Ask any Pomeranian.
A Pomeranian will bark at one snowflake and call it victory.
Two of the three dogs saved from the Titanic were Pomeranians.
Two Pomeranians on a cushion make one warm, fluffy cloud.
lw: The tiny sweater is on, and the leash is ready.

A Pomeranian does not think it is small. It thinks the whole world has been scaled down for its convenience. It steps to the door, chin up, tail high, and waits for you to catch up. The door opens, and the snowy yard is ready to roam.

p: The aristocrat who loves everybody.
s: The Cavalier King Charles Spaniel has a face made for portraits. Silky ears, wide dark eyes, a chestnut and white coat. It looks like royalty because, historically, it was.

These small spaniels warmed the laps of the English court. King Charles II adored them so much that, by Samuel Pepys’s account, he played with his dogs instead of minding the state. The breed carries his name.

Before central heating, a lap spaniel had a job. Ladies of the court called them comforters and held them for warmth. A Cavalier still believes that is its calling. It will curl against you, sigh, and become a small furry heater.

Over the centuries the original style nearly disappeared. In 1926 an American named Roswell Eldridge offered a prize at Crufts for spaniels like those in old royal paintings. Breeders took up the challenge, and the Cavalier returned.

The result is a spaniel with a sweet face and a bottomless supply of affection. Cavaliers befriend children, cats, strangers, and the mail carrier. They are happiest in your lap, or beside it, or on your feet.
Take one home and the arrangement is simple. You supply the sofa. The Cavalier supplies the loyalty, and a small invisible crown.
rc: A royal lap spaniel with a famously open heart (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for King Charles II, who adored toy spaniels. Cavalier sets this breed apart from the flat-faced King Charles Spaniel.
Notable Cavaliers
Rex, Ronald Reagan’s White House companion. The spaniels of King Charles II, who kept them at court.
Good to Know
Wants company all day. Sheds and needs regular brushing. Prone to heart and spine conditions, so choose a breeder who screens carefully.
Coats & Colors
A silky coat in four colors: Blenheim (chestnut and white), tricolor, ruby, and black and tan. The tail wags nonstop.
By the Numbers
Thirteen to eighteen pounds. Four recognized colors. Recognized by the AKC in 1995.
d: The Cavalier sleeps like a monarch who has finished governing.
Cavaliers are named for King Charles II, who adored toy spaniels.
Affection is a full-time job. The Cavalier works every shift.
Samuel Pepys complained the king played with dogs instead of governing.
Ronald Reagan’s White House dog Rex was a Cavalier.
A Cavalier will catch snowflakes on its tongue and call it dessert.
Only the face shows. The rest has gone entirely to blanket.
lw: The leash is by the door, and the world is waiting.

A Cavalier does not demand the walk. It asks politely, with eyes that have melted harder hearts than yours. Then it trots out, ears swinging, delighted with everyone it meets. The door opens, and the kingdom is ready to roam.

p: The gentle philosopher with a scowl.
s: The Bulldog looks like a worried bouncer and behaves like a sleepy philosopher. The wrinkles say stern. The eyes say snack. Together they say character.

The look was built for a rough job. By most tellings, English dogs were bred low, wide, and stubborn to take on bulls in a cruel sport. Parliament banned bull-baiting in 1835, and the breed lost its work.

Then came the great surprise. Breeders kept the shape and rebuilt the temperament. The ferocity faded. What remained was courage, loyalty, and a calm so deep it can pass for sleep. The Bulldog went from the ring to the hearth.
Britain adopted the dog as a national emblem, a symbol of grit and stubborn good humor. Winston Churchill, with his scowl and his bulldog spirit, only made the match tighter.
America joined in. The Bulldog became a mascot for universities, a legend of the Marine Corps, and a star of the screen. Yale’s Handsome Dan has been a living mascot since 1889.

At home, the Bulldog wants three things. A warm spot, a soft cushion, and company. It gives back snores, devotion, and an expression that makes a bad day look silly. Keep it cool, keep it close, and never ask it to hurry.
rc: Stubbornness elevated to an art (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for the bulls it was once bred to face. Bull plus dog. The job is gone, but the name stayed.
Notable Bulldogs
Handsome Dan, Yale’s living mascot since 1889. Uga, the University of Georgia’s white Bulldog. Chesty, the Marine Corps mascot.
Good to Know
Overheats easily and snores. Wrinkles need daily wiping. Breathing and joint problems are common, so choose a breeder who screens carefully.
Coats & Colors
A short, smooth coat in brindle, white, red, fawn, or piebald. A short tail and small rose ears.
By the Numbers
Forty to fifty pounds. Bull-baiting banned in 1835. Recognized by the AKC in 1886.
d: The Bulldog sleeps belly-up, defenseless and entirely at peace.
Parliament banned bull-baiting in 1835. The Bulldog moved indoors.
The armchair is too small. The Bulldog has decided otherwise.
Notice small things, like one snowflake. The Bulldog always does.
Yale’s mascot Handsome Dan has been a Bulldog since 1889.
Churchill’s scowl made the Bulldog a symbol of British grit.
The sweater is on. The mat is claimed. Nobody argues.
lw: The porch light is on, and the doormat is occupied.

A Bulldog does not rush a walk. It considers the weather, the doorway, and the importance of the morning. Then it rolls out, stout and cheerful, to inspect the world at its own pace. The door opens, and the winter is ready to roam.

p: The friend who is always glad to see you.
s: Some dogs are admired. The Golden Retriever is adored. The face says welcome, the tail says everything is wonderful, and the whole body says you were missed, even if you only stepped out for the mail.

The breed began in the Scottish Highlands in the 1800s. Lord Tweedmouth wanted a retriever that could fetch game over rough ground and cold water, then carry it home unharmed. He bred his yellow retrievers with care and kept careful notes.
The result was a dog with a water-shedding coat, a soft mouth, and a mind eager to please. The AKC recognized the breed in 1925.
Then the work widened. Goldens became guide dogs, search partners, therapy visitors, and patient listeners beside children learning to read. Wherever people need comfort, a Golden seems to arrive.
America took the breed to heart. Presidents kept them. Films starred them. Year after year, they rank among the nation’s favorite dogs.
At home, a Golden asks for little. A walk, a toy, a family. It will bring you a stick, a shoe, or a stuffed bear, and then look proud. Keep it close, keep it busy, and expect to be loved.
rc: The gold standard of friendliness (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Golden for the color of the coat. Retriever for the job of fetching shot game from land and water.
Notable Golden Retrievers
Liberty, President Ford’s White House companion. Shadow, the wise voice of Homeward Bound. Buddy, the star of Air Bud.
Good to Know
Sheds year-round and loves to chew. Needs daily exercise and daily company. Choose a breeder who screens hips, elbows, eyes, and heart.
Coats & Colors
A dense, water-repellent coat with feathering on the chest, legs, and tail. Shades from light cream to deep gold.
By the Numbers
Fifty-five to seventy-five pounds. Developed in Scotland in the 1800s. Recognized by the AKC in 1925.
d: The fire is warm, the bear is close, and all is well.
Lord Tweedmouth bred the first Goldens in Scotland in the 1800s.
Winter is not weather. To a Golden, it is a toy.
A soft mouth means a Golden can carry a stick gently.
Rest your head by the window. The snow will wait for you.
Golden puppies often darken with age. Cream today, gold tomorrow.
The snow flies, the tail wags, and joy is everywhere.
lw: The leash is by the door, and the lantern is lit.

A Golden never needs convincing. It needs only the sound of the door. Then out it bounds, gold against the snow, sure the best part of the day has just begun. The gate swings open, and the world is ready to roam.

p: The Irish farmhand with a silk coat and a spring in its step.
s: Most terriers wear armor. The Wheaten wears silk. That one difference tells you where it came from and how it behaves.
The breed began on Irish farms, where a dog had to earn its supper. It herded cattle, guarded the house, and cleared the barn of rats. Nobody bred it for a show ring. Nobody had the time.
Its coat is the trademark. Soft, wavy, and the color of ripening wheat, it sheds little and tangles easily. Puppies are born darker. The wheat color comes with age.

The temperament is a terrier’s, turned friendly. A Wheaten is busy, bold, and bright. It is also the one terrier that greets strangers like old friends. Owners call it the Wheaten greetin’, a bouncing hello that can reach the top of a doorframe.
That bounce needs exercise. A bored Wheaten invents its own jobs, and you will not approve of them.
Give it a walk, a brush, and a family. You get sunny, sturdy devotion with the energy of a farm dog and the heart of a lapdog.
rc: Ireland’s soft-coated farm all-rounder (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for its soft, wheat-colored coat, rare among terriers. It was the all-purpose working dog of the Irish farm.
A Softer Terrier
It shares ancestry with Ireland’s other terriers but trades the harsh jacket for silk. The Irish Kennel Club recognized it in 1937.
Good to Know
Lively and outgoing. Needs daily exercise and company. The coat needs regular brushing to avoid mats. Low-shedding, which many owners prize.
Coats & Colors
A single coat, soft and gently waving, in shades of wheat from pale beige to gold. Dark puppy coats clear as the dog matures.
By the Numbers
Seventeen to nineteen inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1973. Five or six puppies to a litter.
d: Rain on the window, a warm stove, and an old dog with nothing left to prove.
A Wheaten has a single soft coat. No woolly undercoat, so it sheds little.
Irish farm dogs worked from dawn to dusk. The Wheaten herded, guarded, and ratted.
Wheaten puppies are born dark. The wheat color arrives slowly, often by age two.
When the day is too much, put your head in a boot and wag. It helps.
The Irish Kennel Club recognized the Wheaten in 1937. The AKC followed in 1973.
A basin, a wool blanket, and a heap of sleepy puppies. Farm life at its best.
lw: The door is open, and the lantern is lit.

A Wheaten greets the end of the day the way it greeted the start. Tail up, ears forward, sure that something good is coming. Old Seamus sits on the step and watches the first stars. Tomorrow there will be another hello.

p: The bird dog that springs first and apologizes never.
s: The Springer does not walk into a field. It springs into it. Every part of the breed is built for that first burst.

The name tells the job. In England, spaniels worked ahead of the hunter and sprang, or flushed, game birds from cover. The Springer did it with a wagging tail and a face that said this was the best day ever.
Cockers and field spaniels were once born in the same litters. Size and work sorted them out. The Springer became the bigger, longer-legged one.

The breed later split in two. A leaner field type stayed in the woods. A fuller-coated show type moved to the ring. Today they can look like different dogs with one name. The AKC recognized the breed in 1910.
At home the Springer is sunny, eager, and sticky. It follows you from room to room. It wants a job and your company. Left alone too long, it grows anxious.
Give it a long walk, a stick to carry, and a family to love. A Springer will take it from there.
rc: The flushing spaniel that springs game (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
From its job of springing, or flushing, game birds out of cover. Cockers and field spaniels once shared its litters.
A Breed Split in Two
A leaner field type and a fuller-coated show type drifted so far apart that they look like different dogs. Both are Springers.
Good to Know
Needs daily exercise and a job. Can grow anxious when left alone. Long ears need regular checks and cleaning.
Coats & Colors
A feathered double coat, usually liver and white or black and white, sometimes with tan points. Made to shed water and push through brush.
By the Numbers
Nineteen to twenty inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1910. Five to seven puppies to a litter.
d: Easter morning, a basket of dyed eggs, and one dog guarding one egg.
Springers can work all day. The breed was made for brush and water, dawn to dusk.
Millie, a Springer in the Bush White House, “wrote” a bestselling book.
Springers work as detection dogs. A flushing nose is a finding nose.
Greet every duck as a friend. Most will disagree. Keep wagging.
Field and show Springers share a name. Side by side, they look like two breeds.
A puppy asleep in an upturned flat cap, and a weathered hand that does not dare move.
lw: The Easter basket is empty, and the evening is quiet.

Barley lies by the garden path, the last egg between his paws. A cottage window glows. A Springer’s day is built from big moments. This is the small one, the long breath after, when everyone is home and nobody has to move.

p: A nose with a dog attached, and no off switch.
s: The Beagle is mostly nose. The rest of the dog is there to carry it.
English hunters bred the breed to follow rabbits on foot. A pack worked together, heads down, voices up. The AKC recognized the Beagle in 1885.
That nose holds around 220 million scent receptors. A person has about six million. Give a Beagle a trail and the rest of the world disappears.
It still works for a living. The USDA Beagle Brigade sniffs out smuggled fruit and meat in airport baggage. The breed was chosen for the nose, and for a face no traveler minds meeting.
Fame came too. Snoopy made the silhouette a star. Uno won Best in Show at Westminster in 2008, the first Beagle ever to do it. Miss P won it again in 2015.
Living with one means living with the nose. A Beagle on a scent is deaf to you. It needs a fence, patience, and a latched pantry.
rc: America’s favorite scent hound (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Likely from the old French begueule, a loud mouth, or the Celtic beag, small. Either fits.
Notable Beagles
Snoopy, the world’s best-known cartoon dog. Uno, Best in Show at Westminster in 2008. Miss P, in 2015.
Good to Know
The nose rules the dog. Off leash, a Beagle follows a trail over the horizon. Needs a fence, company, and watching at mealtimes.
A Working Nose
The USDA Beagle Brigade screens airport baggage for food and contraband. A world-class nose and a face too friendly to alarm anyone.
By the Numbers
Recognized by the AKC in 1885. About six puppies to a litter. A top-ten American breed for most of the last century.
d: Morning sun, an open screen door, and an old hound with a well-earned nap.
A Beagle has about 220 million scent receptors. You have around six million.
Uno won Westminster in 2008 and bayed at the crowd all the way around the ring.
The USDA Beagle Brigade finds smuggled fruit in airport suitcases.
Every storm ends. Sit by the door and keep your nose ready.
Legend says Queen Elizabeth I kept tiny pocket beagles, small enough for a saddlebag.
A gentle hand on an old head, and a porch swing that keeps the rhythm.
lw: The rain taps the window, and the lamp is low.
A Beagle ends the day curled close to its oldest friend. The nose finally rests. The tail finally stills. Outside, the town is damp and quiet. Inside, two dogs and a blanket make a small, warm world.

p: Half a dog tall, twice a dog brave.
s: The Dachshund was built for a fight underground. German foresters wanted a dog that could follow a badger down its tunnel and not back out.

The name says so. Dachs is badger. Hund is dog. Every odd thing about the shape is on purpose. Short legs keep the nose near the ground. The long body fits the burrow. The big bark carries up through the earth.
There are two sizes and three coats. Smooth, long, and wire. Red, cream, black and tan, dapple, and more. Each coat type seems to bring its own temper.
The shape even named a meal. German immigrants sold sausages that looked like the breed. By most tellings, that is how America got the hot dog.
The personality is far larger than the dog. A Dachshund is brave to the point of nonsense, stubborn as a stain, and certain it is in charge. You do not own a Dachshund. You are assigned to one.
Look after that long back. Skip the big jumps and the long stairs. Offer a hand up and a ramp.
rc: A top-five American favorite (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Dachshund is German for badger dog, from Dachs, badger, and Hund, dog. The name is a job description.
Notable Dachshunds
Waldi, the first official Olympic mascot, Munich, 1972. Famous owners include Picasso, Andy Warhol, and E. B. White.
Good to Know
One breed, two sizes, three coats. The long back needs care. Too many stairs and big jumps are hard on it, so offer a hand up.
Coats & Colors
Red, cream, black and tan, chocolate and tan, blue, dapple, brindle, and piebald. Smooth, long, or wire.
By the Numbers
Recognized by the AKC in 1885, among its earliest breeds. Bred to take on prey far heavier than itself.
d: A wicker basket, a sunny balcony, and a senior Dachshund who has claimed both.
Dachshund is German for badger dog. The name is a job description.
Waldi, a Dachshund, was the first official mascot in Olympic history. Munich, 1972.
Smooth, long, and wire coats share one breed. Each tends to have its own attitude.
Look at the stairs. Do the math. Ask for a lift. There is no shame in a ramp.
The hot dog is said to be named for the Dachshund. The sausage looked like the dog.
Two friends, one knitted blanket, and rain on the glass. Noses touching.
lw: A paper lantern glows, and the canal is quiet.

A Dachshund is rarely quiet. But at dusk, on a towpath, it walks slow and long. Low to the ground, nose to the stones, it reads the day one last time. Then home, a blanket, and the end of a large little life.

p: A fisherman’s deckhand that traded the boat for the White House lawn.
s: The Portuguese Water Dog earned its living on the Atlantic. Along the coast of Portugal, fishermen kept these curly, athletic dogs as crew.
The dogs herded fish into nets. They retrieved lost tackle. They carried messages between boats and from ship to shore. The dog was a deckhand with a tail.
Everything about it is built for the sea. Webbed feet. A waterproof curly coat. A strong swimming stroke. The low-shedding coat is a bonus for the people who live with it now.
The breed nearly vanished with the old fishing life. A few devoted breeders pulled it back. It is still uncommon. The AKC recognized it in 1983.
Then it found the most famous of homes. The Obama family chose Portuguese Water Dogs, Bo and later Sunny. For eight years the breed served as America’s First Dogs.
The temperament suits both jobs. Bright, energetic, and affectionate. A tireless worker that needs exercise and company. The same willing deckhand, now happiest at your side.
rc: A fisherman’s diver and First Family pet (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for its homeland and trade. On Portugal’s coast it herded fish into nets and carried messages between boats.
America’s First Dog
Bo and Sunny, the Obama family’s Portuguese Water Dogs, chosen partly for the low-shedding coat. First Dogs for eight years.
Good to Know
Needs real exercise, mental work, and company. The curly coat sheds little but needs regular grooming. Loves water above all.
Coats & Colors
A dense, curly or wavy waterproof coat in black, brown, white, or combinations. Often clipped in a working lion trim.
By the Numbers
Recognized by the AKC in 1983. About seven puppies to a litter. Once near extinction, now beloved but uncommon.
d: Cool tile, a shaded door, and a bowl of water. Salgado has the best seat in the village.
Webbed feet make the Portuguese Water Dog a strong swimmer. The curly coat sheds little.
Bo and Sunny made the breed a First Dog. Eight years on the White House lawn.
Portuguese fishermen sent these dogs overboard with messages, boat to boat.
It is Earth Day. Kneel at a tide pool. Everything small is doing important work.
The breed nearly vanished with the old fishing fleets. A few breeders saved it.
A puppy asleep in a fish basket among the oranges, and a vendor’s steady hands.
lw: The boats rock, and the harbor lights come on.

Two dogs walk the quay, one gray at the muzzle and one still bouncing. The old one sets the pace. The younger one lets him. Salt on the air, rope on the stones, and the last of the light on the water.

p: The drover’s right hand, tireless, clever, and faintly bossy.
s: The Australian Cattle Dog was built to move stubborn cattle across an enormous, brutal country.

Nineteenth-century drovers needed a dog tough enough for punishing heat and long distances. They crossed their herding dogs with the wild dingo and added dashes of collie and Dalmatian. Out came a compact, weatherproof powerhouse.
It works the way a good foreman works. It drives stock from behind, nips at heels, and ducks the kicks. That earned it the nickname heeler, blue or red by the speckle of its coat.
It also holds a record. A Cattle Dog named Bluey lived to twenty-nine, the oldest verified age for any dog. The AKC recognized the breed in 1980.
All that drive needs an outlet. The Cattle Dog is intelligent, intense, and deeply loyal. It is not a dog for a quiet home. A bored heeler will manage your household whether you asked it to or not.
Give it a job and it gives you everything. It bonds hard to one or two people and watches over them with a drover’s seriousness.
rc: The Australian drover’s dog (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for the job and the country. Also called the blue or red heeler, for its speckled coat and its habit of nipping heels.
The Oldest Dog Ever
A Cattle Dog named Bluey lived twenty-nine years, the longest-lived dog on record.
Good to Know
Bred to work all day in hard country. Needs serious exercise and a job. A bored Cattle Dog herds, nips, and manages the household.
Coats & Colors
A short, dense, weatherproof coat in blue or red speckle, often with patches and a mask.
By the Numbers
Recognized by the AKC in 1980. About five puppies to a litter. A favorite for dog sports and ranch work.
d: A sunny verandah, a pair of work boots, and a dog who is, for once, off duty.
Cattle Dogs drive stock from behind, nipping heels. Hence the name, heeler.
Bluey, a Cattle Dog, lived to twenty-nine. No dog has been verified older.
Cattle Dog puppies are born white. The blue or red speckles come as they grow.
Even a laughing kookaburra deserves a good listen. Not everything needs a reply.
Drovers crossed herding dogs with the dingo. The cross gave the breed its toughness.
A weathered hand rests on an old head. Neither of them says a word.
lw: The fire is low, and the sky is full of stars.
Two heelers sit on the tray of the ute, one old and one young. The Milky Way arcs overhead. A Cattle Dog works until the work is done. Tonight the work is done. The stars have the watch.

p: The smartest dog in the room, and it knows it.
s: The Border Collie is widely called the most intelligent breed alive. It has the work ethic to back the claim.
It was bred in the border hills between England and Scotland to herd sheep. It does so with an uncanny, crouching stare known as the eye. A whole flock bends to it.
The mind is startling. A Border Collie named Chaser learned the names of more than a thousand objects. She could fetch each one on command.
That brilliance is a responsibility. A Border Collie needs a job, hard exercise, and a problem to solve every day. A bored one will invent work. Children, cars, and shadows are all fair game.
The breed excels at nearly everything. It dominates herding trials, agility, and flying-disc contests. The AKC recognized it in 1995, long after shepherds had settled its reputation.
For the right person it is unmatched. Devoted, sensitive, and tuned to every signal. Give it a task and a partner and you have the finest working mind in dogdom.
rc: Widely called the world’s smartest breed (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for the border country between England and Scotland. Collie is an old word for the herding dogs of the British hills.
The Cleverest Dog
Routinely ranked the most intelligent breed. Chaser learned over a thousand object names, a record for a dog.
Good to Know
Built to work all day. Without a job and hard exercise it grows anxious and destructive. Needs an active owner.
The Eye
A low, crouching stare steers livestock without force. Pet Border Collies will herd people and pets alike.
By the Numbers
Recognized by the AKC in 1995. Four to eight puppies to a litter. Champion of herding trials and most dog sports.
d: Peat smoke, a dented kettle, and an old dog who has finally been told he can stop.
The eye is a low, hard stare. A Border Collie can steer a flock without a bark.
Chaser learned the names of more than a thousand toys. She could fetch each one by name.
Border Collies herd without being asked. Ducks, children, and the occasional lawnmower.
Sit still on the machine. Watch the whole hill. Decide before you move.
The breed is named for the border country between England and Scotland.
Eight puppies tumble over one patient old dog. He is too kind to stand up.
lw: The lantern is low, and the lambing shed is quiet.

Fly lies in the straw. A newborn lamb sleeps against her warm side. She has been up all night. She will be up again tomorrow. A Border Collie’s work is never really done. But for one hour, in lantern light, keeping watch is enough.

p: The shepherd of the hills who grew up to be a movie star.
s: The Collie spent centuries as a working shepherd in the hills of Scotland and northern England. It was valued for brains and a gentle, biddable nature, not for looks.

Royalty changed its fortunes. Queen Victoria fell for the breed on a visit to Scotland and brought Collies to her court. Fashion followed the queen. A humble herder became an elegant showpiece with a flowing mane.

Then a fictional dog made it immortal. Lassie, in books, films, and a long-running television series, became one of the most famous animals in the world. She was the loyal dog who always found her way home.
The temperament earned the affection. The Collie is sweet, sensitive, and devoted. It is famously good with children and eager to please. It herds its family with quiet care.
The thick coat needs regular grooming. The AKC recognized the breed in 1885.
Beneath the glamour beats a shepherd’s heart. The Collie still watches over its people with the patient attention it once gave the flock.
rc: Shepherd of the hills and TV’s Lassie (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
An old Scottish word for a sheepdog, likely tied to the black-faced colley sheep. Rough and smooth coats.
Lassie’s Breed
The fictional Collie Lassie, in books, film, and television, became the breed’s enduring ambassador.
Good to Know
Gentle, sensitive, and good with children. Needs moderate exercise and regular grooming. Some carry a drug sensitivity worth a vet’s note.
Coats & Colors
The rough Collie has a long, flowing coat and full mane, the smooth a shorter one. Sable and white, tricolor, blue merle, white.
By the Numbers
Recognized by the AKC in 1885. About eight puppies to a litter. Popularized by Queen Victoria and Lassie.
d: Mother’s Day morning. A tartan blanket, a rainy window, and the family guardian.
The Collie comes in two coats. The rough has the mane. The smooth has the speed.
Queen Victoria loved the Collies she met in Scotland. Fashion followed the queen.
Lassie was played by a male dog. Pal and his descendants wore the role for decades.
Lean on the rail and watch the gulls. You do not have to chase everything.
Many Collies carry a gene that makes them sensitive to some drugs. Vets know to check.
Mothers know the quiet. Four sable pups curl into one warm circle.
lw: The posy is in a jar, and the boots are by the door.

Bonnie rests her chin on a small pair of muddy wellies. Someone has been out in the puddles, and someone has come home. A Collie’s whole job, in the end, is to count heads and keep them close. Tonight the count is right.

p: The merry little gun dog who became everyone’s sweetheart.
s: The Cocker Spaniel is the smallest of the sporting dogs and one of the oldest names on the American rolls.

Spaniels came to England from the continent centuries ago and split by job. The smallest were used to flush woodcock from cover. That work gave the Cocker its name. It was one of the first nine breeds recognized in America, in 1878.
In America it took its own path. Breeders here favored a smaller, rounder, more glamorous dog, with a domed head and a long, feathered coat. In time the American Cocker became its own breed.
Then it became a star. By the mid-twentieth century the Cocker was among the most popular dogs in the country. Lady, an animated Cocker, charmed a generation in a beloved film.
The temperament earned the fame. Gentle, merry, and eager to please. A tail that rarely stops. The long ears and silky coat ask for steady grooming.
Beneath the glamour beats a bird dog’s heart. The Cocker still loves to use its nose and please its person.
rc: One of America’s first nine breeds, 1878 (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
From the woodcock, the game bird the smallest spaniels flushed. The American Cocker later became its own breed.
America’s Sweetheart
In the 1940s and 1950s the Cocker was among America’s most popular breeds. Lady, in the animated film, sealed it.
Good to Know
Merry, gentle, and thrives on attention. Long ears and a silky coat need regular care. Buy from breeders who screen eyes and ears.
Coats & Colors
A silky, feathered coat in many colors, from buff and black to parti-color and roan. A real grooming commitment.
By the Numbers
One of the nine charter breeds recognized in 1878. About five puppies to a litter.
d: A wing chair, a teacup, and an open book. The dog has read the first page and approves.
The name comes from the woodcock. The smallest spaniels were used to flush the bird.
Lady, the Cocker in Lady and the Tramp, charmed a generation. Spaghetti did the rest.
The Cocker was among America’s favorite dogs in the 1940s and 1950s.
Plant something small. Check on it every day. Wait.
England and America each kept a Cocker. The two grew into separate breeds.
Three puppies, one wheelbarrow, and a garden of flowers. The gardener will be a while.
lw: The string lights come on, and the garden goes quiet.

A Cocker on a bench is a small portrait of patience. Ears like silk, eyes like warm tea. The day’s work is done. The garden has been supervised. All that remains is to sit, be adored, and be glad of it.

p: A genius in fancy dress, and it knows it.
s: The Poodle is German, whatever the accent suggests. It was bred along the rivers of Germany to retrieve shot ducks from cold water. The name admits it. Pudel comes from an old word for splashing about.
Even the absurd show clip began as work kit. Puffs of coat stayed over the joints and chest to keep them warm in the water. The rest was shaved to cut the drag.
France took one look and claimed it forever. The Poodle became the darling of the circus and the court. The world still files it as French by mistake.
Under the topiary is an athlete. One breed comes in three sizes, Standard, Miniature, and Toy, sorted by height alone.

It is also, by most accounts, the second cleverest dog alive, behind only the Border Collie. A Poodle learns fast, forgets nothing, and bores quickly. Leave one idle and it will appoint itself a project.
For all the dignity, the Poodle is a clown on purpose. Springy, theatrical, and stuck to its people like a shadow. You do not train a Poodle so much as negotiate with it.
rc: A top-ten American favorite for decades (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
The name is German, not French. Pudel comes from pudeln, to splash in water, after the breed’s first job retrieving ducks.
Notable Poodles
Sage, a Miniature Poodle, won Best in Show at Westminster in 2024. The breed has won the title many times.
Good to Know
The show clip was once practical. Puffs of coat kept joints warm in the water. Behind the grooming is a working water dog.
Coats, Colors & Sizes
A dense, curly, low-shedding coat in many colors. One breed in three sizes, Standard, Miniature, and Toy, by height alone.
By the Numbers
Often ranked second most intelligent, behind the Border Collie. Recognized by the AKC in 1887.
d: A velvet cushion, a fire-escape window, and a dog who has retired from the city.
Poodle comes from the German Pudel, to splash. The breed began as a duck retriever.
Sage, a Miniature Poodle, won Best in Show at Westminster in 2024.
The fancy clip was practical. Pom-poms kept joints warm. The shaved parts cut drag.
Stand at a bakery window. Breathe. Some days the best plan is to look at pastry.
Cross a Poodle with anything and you get a doodle. The Poodle is the clever half.
Two tiny puppies sleep in a hatbox lined with silk. The city can wait.
lw: The brownstone windows glow, and the street is quiet.

Peaches trots ahead under the clipped trees. Old Pearl keeps the pace she likes. A Poodle in the city is a small, proud parade. Tonight it is a parade of two, heading home to a warm door and a soft chair.

p: Some dogs notice things. German Shepherds notice everything.
s: The German Shepherd is a young breed with an old purpose. In 1899 a German cavalry officer, Max von Stephanitz, set out to build the ideal working dog. He prized brains over ribbons.
The first dog he registered, Horand, founded the line. Nearly every Shepherd alive traces back to that one choice.

The pasture was only the start. Within a generation the breed had traded herding for the police beat, the battlefield, and the rescue site. It guides the blind. It finds what is hidden. It works the rubble after the worst days.
Fame came early. In 1918 an American soldier found a litter of pups in a bombed kennel in France. One, Rin Tin Tin, became a Hollywood star and made the breed a household name.
The mind is the marvel. A Shepherd reads a situation, weighs it, and decides. It is confident without being reckless and protective without being cruel.
Give it a job and a person to do it for. A bored Shepherd writes its own job description, and you may not like the terms.
rc: The definitive police and service dog (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Plain and literal: the German shepherd dog. After World War I the AKC dropped German for years, and Britain used Alsatian.
Notable German Shepherds
Rin Tin Tin, a Hollywood star from 1918. Buddy, America’s first Seeing Eye dog, guiding Morris Frank in 1928.
Good to Know
Bred to work, so a bored Shepherd invents a job. Needs exercise, training, and company. Sheds hard. Good breeders screen hips and elbows.
Coats & Colors
A dense double coat that sheds year-round. Black and tan, sable, solid black, and bi-color.
By the Numbers
About eight puppies to a litter. Recognized by the AKC in 1908. By most counts the world’s most used police and military dog.
d: Max von Stephanitz registered Horand in 1899. Nearly every Shepherd descends from him.
Memorial Day. The breed has served beside soldiers and police for a century. Say thanks.
Rin Tin Tin was found in a bombed kennel in France in 1918. He became a Hollywood star.
After World War I the AKC called the breed just the Shepherd Dog. Britain said Alsatian.
A branch twice your size is still just a branch. Pick it up. Carry it home.
Buddy, a German Shepherd, became America’s first Seeing Eye dog in 1928.
Puppies climb over old Bear as if he were a mountain. He lets them.
lw: The flag stirs, and the road is quiet.

Ranger stops at the fence post and looks back. He is checking that you are still there. A Shepherd never really goes off duty. One ear is always up. The mountains turn gold behind him. Everyone is accounted for. Now he can walk on.

p: The velcro dog, a rust-gold hunter that cannot bear to leave your side.
s: The Vizsla is one of the oldest pointing breeds and one of the most devoted. It comes from Hungary, where it hunted beside the Magyar nobility for centuries.
It was an all-purpose gun dog. It could point game and retrieve it from land or water. Its image turns up in Hungarian art going back hundreds of years.

It nearly vanished more than once. War and upheaval in the twentieth century brought the breed close to extinction. Dedicated breeders rebuilt it from a small surviving group. The AKC recognized it in 1960.
The look is distinctive and warm. A short, sleek coat in one shade of golden rust, with a nose and eyes to match.
It earned a nickname for its clinginess. The Vizsla is famously a velcro dog. It attaches to its person with an intensity that can tip into anxiety if it is left alone too much.
Give it exercise and closeness. It will hunt all day and then press against you all evening, and it cannot understand why anyone would want to be in a different room.
rc: Hungary’s velcro gun dog (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Vizsla is simply the Hungarian word for the breed, a pointing gun dog of the Magyar nobility, pictured in art for centuries.
Back from the Brink
The breed nearly died out amid the wars of the twentieth century and was rebuilt from a small surviving group.
Good to Know
A velcro dog that bonds hard and suffers when left alone. Needs serious exercise and close human company.
Coats & Colors
A short, smooth, easy-care coat in solid golden rust, with matching nose and eyes. Little undercoat, so it feels the cold.
By the Numbers
Recognized by the AKC in 1960. Six to eight puppies to a litter. A steady climber as hunter and housemate.
d: A sleeper on the sofa, and a rust-gold dog pressed against the legs. No gap allowed.
Vizsla is Hungarian for the breed. Vizslas appear in Hungarian art for centuries.
War nearly erased the breed. A few devoted breeders rebuilt it from a handful of dogs.
Vizslas are called velcro dogs. They will follow you to the bathroom and wait.
Put your nose to a gentle horse. Some friendships need no words.
A Vizsla has little undercoat. It feels the cold and finds the warm blanket first.
Puppies asleep on the firewood, one nose in a work boot. The farmhand smiles.
lw: The hay bales cast long shadows, and the gravel road is warm.
Cooper and Willow trot side by side, shoulders touching. A Vizsla hates a gap. Even walking, it leans. The sky goes peach. The prairie hums. Everyone is close, so everything is fine.

p: The dog that does everything and still just wants to please you.
s: The Labrador never set foot in Labrador. It grew up on the docks of Newfoundland, where fishermen kept a short-coated water dog to haul nets and fetch fish that slipped the line.

British sportsmen watched it work. They shipped a few home in the 1800s and bred the finest gun dog in the field. The job left its mark. Webbed feet. A thick otter tail for a rudder. A coat that beads water like a raincoat.
Almost anything you ask of a Lab, it does well and gladly. Labs guide the blind and hear for the deaf. They sniff out explosives and the early warning of a seizure. They pull children from pools.
The genius is the mouth. A Lab can carry a raw egg across a yard and set it down without a dent. Add a bottomless wish to please and you get a dog that is almost embarrassingly easy to teach.
Off duty, it is pure appetite and affection. It will eat what it should not. It will lean its full weight on your leg. It will treat every visitor as a friend it has not met yet.
America agreed for thirty-one years in a row. The Lab was the No. 1 breed from 1991 to 2021, and it is still No. 2. Gentle, tireless, and sure the next good thing is coming. Usually it involves food.
rc: No. 1 for 31 years, now No. 2 (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
A geographic mix-up that stuck. The breed descends from the St. John’s water dog of Newfoundland. British breeders named it for the wrong coast.
Notable Labradors
Endal, a British assistance dog who loaded washing machines. Jake, a search dog at Ground Zero. Zanjeer, who found explosives in Mumbai, 1993.
Good to Know
Bred to work all day, so a bored Lab invents its own job. Many carry a hunger gene, so portions matter. The coat sheds.
Coats, Colors & Tail
A dense, water-repellent double coat in black, yellow, or chocolate, all in one litter. The otter tail steers like a rudder.
By the Numbers
About seven puppies to a litter. Recognized by the AKC in 1917. No. 1 in America for thirty-one years.
d: A screened porch, a daybed, and a paperback. The dog is saving the spot.
Labs have webbed toes and an otter tail. Both help them swim.
Endal, a British assistance dog, could load a washing machine and use a cash machine.
A Lab litter can hold black, yellow, and chocolate puppies. Three colors, one family.
Check the bucket. Check the dock. Most days the best thing is just beyond your nose.
Labs held the No. 1 spot in America for thirty-one years. Then came the Frenchie.
Puppies piled in a red wagon beside the lake. All the way down to the dock and back.
lw: The lights come on along the dock, and the lake goes pink.
Hank and old Tucker walk toward the water, side by side. The young dog slows for the old one. A Lab knows this part by heart. The long day ends at the edge of the lake, and the lake is still.

p: The clown who never grew up and never wants to.
s: A Boxer does not walk into a room. It arrives. The whole back end wiggles, the front paws pat the air, and the face says the party can finally start.

The breed took shape in Germany in the late 1800s. Breeders in Munich crossed the old Bullenbeisser, a big-game hunting dog, with the English Bulldog. They wanted strength, courage, and a short muzzle that could hold on.
They got all of that. They also got a clown. Boxers stay playful for years. People call them the Peter Pan of dogs, and the name fits.
Boxers carried messages and stood guard in the world wars. American soldiers brought them home, and the breed took off. The AKC recognized it in 1904.
At home, a Boxer is half guard and half goof. It watches the door like a sentry, then licks the visitor. It leans, it snorts, and it dances the kidney bean, curving its whole body in joy.
Give a Boxer exercise, shade, and a seat near you. It will repay you in wiggles. It never forgets Father’s Day.
rc: The Peter Pan of dogs, forever playful (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
No one is sure. The likeliest story is the way a Boxer bats with its front paws, as if sparring.
Notable Boxers
Dampf von Dom, the first AKC champion Boxer, in 1915. Boxers also carried messages for the German army in World War I.
Good to Know
Flat faces overheat fast, so shade and water matter. Boxers can inherit heart disease, so ask about screening.
Coats & Colors
A sleek, short coat in fawn or brindle, often with white markings. Mostly white Boxers are not allowed in the show ring.
By the Numbers
Fifty to eighty pounds. Created in Germany in the late 1800s. Recognized by the AKC in 1904.
d: Father’s Day. The old Boxer has the porch glider, and nobody will argue.
The Boxer began in Munich, from the old Bullenbeisser and the English Bulldog.
Boxers carried messages in World War I. Brave dogs, and still silly at home.
A Boxer’s jaw looks fierce. Its soul is a marshmallow. Guard the hot dogs anyway.
Stop at the zinnias. Watch the bee. Nothing needs you for a full minute.
Short noses mean Boxers overheat fast. Keep the hose handy.
Puppies pile into Dad’s empty chair. He will sit somewhere else tonight.
lw: The porch lights come on, and the fireflies rise.

Rocky and Roxie walk the cul-de-sac side by side. She skips. He plods. Both tails keep time like metronomes. A Boxer ends the day the way it began, wiggling. Someone left a light on. Home is two doors away.

p: Short legs, big ears, and a herder’s heart.
s: The Pembroke Welsh Corgi is a cattle dog that forgot to grow tall. It never noticed. It herds anything that moves, and a few things that do not.
The breed comes from Pembrokeshire, in Wales. Farmers there kept low dogs to drive cattle. A Corgi nips at the heels, then ducks under the kick. Short legs are a survival skill.
Welsh legend says fairies rode Corgis like horses. The saddle markings on the shoulders prove it. The fairies have not commented.
The Pembroke reached America in the 1930s, and the AKC recognized it in 1934. Then a young princess got one for her birthday, and the whole world took notice.
At home, a Corgi is a big dog in a small package. It barks to announce the mail. It circles your ankles when the family walks in different directions. It is only trying to keep everyone together.
Give it a job, a fence, and a beach. Watch the waistline. A Corgi will eat your whole lunch and look surprised.
rc: Wales’s low-slung cattle dog (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Cor means dwarf and ci means dog in Welsh. Pembroke is the county where the breed took shape.
Notable Corgis
Susan, Queen Elizabeth II’s first Corgi, an 18th birthday gift in 1944. The Queen kept more than thirty over her reign.
Good to Know
Herding instinct means ankle nipping and barking. Short backs need care, so skip high jumps. Corgis shed all year.
Coats & Colors
A thick double coat in red, sable, fawn, or tricolor, with white markings. The tail is short or docked.
By the Numbers
Twenty-five to thirty pounds. Ten to twelve inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1934.
d: Under the umbrella, old Waffles has claimed the best towel. Rank has privileges.
The name means dwarf dog in Welsh. A fair description, and a proud one.
Cape Hatteras Lighthouse is the tallest brick one in America. The Corgi shrugs.
A Corgi will herd a wave. The wave never listens. The Corgi never stops.
Meet the ghost crab nose to nose. Both freeze first. That is respect.
Susan, the Queen’s first Corgi, arrived in 1944. A birthday gift started a dynasty.
Puppies guard a sandcastle moat. The tide will win. They will bark anyway.
lw: The tide goes out, and the sky turns peach.
Waffles walks slow. Biscuit walks slower, on purpose. Their shadows stretch long across the wet sand, two short dogs and two tall shadows. Tomorrow is the Fourth. Tonight is only this.

p: An American cowboy with a mysterious Australian name.
s: The Australian Shepherd is not from Australia. It is as American as a rodeo, and it was born on Western ranches.
The name came from Basque shepherds who reached the American West by way of Australia in the 1800s. Ranchers saw their dogs work, and the name stuck. So did the dogs.

They were bred to herd sheep and cattle across big country. They needed brains, stamina, and an eye for the whole flock. The breed has all three, plus a coat in four colors and eyes that sometimes do not match.
Rodeos made the Aussie a star in the 1950s and 1960s. Trick dogs jumped, balanced, and stole the show. The AKC recognized the breed in 1991.
Today Aussies guide the blind, search for the lost, and visit the sick. At home, they herd children, cats, and the vacuum cleaner. An Aussie with no job will invent one.
Give it a task, a field, and a family to keep track of. It will watch over all of it, and it will watch you most.
rc: A cowboy’s dog with a mistaken name (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Basque shepherds reached America by way of Australia. Ranchers called their dogs Australian Shepherds. The name outlasted the story.
Notable Aussies
Jay Sisler’s rodeo dogs, who dazzled crowds with tricks in the 1950s and 1960s. Aussies also work as guide and search dogs.
Good to Know
Brilliant and busy, so a bored Aussie herds the family. Breeders avoid pairing two merles, which risks deafness and blindness.
Coats & Colors
A medium double coat in blue merle, red merle, black, or red. Eyes may be blue, brown, amber, or one of each.
By the Numbers
Forty to sixty-five pounds. Developed in the American West. Recognized by the AKC in 1991.
d: Independence Day. Old Tex sleeps through the parade. He has seen enough of them.
Not Australian at all. The Aussie was built on American ranches.
Fireworks light the valley. Dusty watches every burst. He counts the flock anyway.
Aussie eyes can be blue, brown, amber, or one of each. Both work fine.
A pink nose and a good slice of watermelon. That is a complete summer.
Aussies love to catch things. A water balloon never stood a chance.
Puppies on a flag quilt. One asleep on Tex’s paw. He will not move it.
lw: The smoke drifts, and the dirt road glows pink.
Dusty and Sage walk home after the fireworks. Her ears still twitch at every echo. He walks a step ahead and checks back. It is an old habit. A herder counts heads, and tonight all heads are home.

p: The Gray Ghost with eyes like amber glass.
s: A Weimaraner moves like smoke. Silver coat, amber eyes, and no sound at all. It does not walk up to you. It appears.

The breed began in Weimar, Germany, in the early 1800s. Grand Duke Karl August and his court wanted a fast, fearless hunter for deer, boar, and bear. Nobles guarded the breed closely and rarely sold a dog.
Later the dogs turned to birds, and the Weimaraner became a versatile gun dog. It points, tracks, and retrieves. The AKC recognized the breed in 1943.
Then it became a star. Photographer William Wegman posed his Weimaraners in costume for decades and made them art-world royalty. President Eisenhower kept one named Heidi at the White House.
At home, a Weimaraner is a shadow with opinions. It follows you from room to room. It loves its people so much that being alone feels like a punishment. It needs miles of running every day.
Give it a lake, a long trail, and a job, and you will have a steady ghost at your heel for life.
rc: The Gray Ghost of German nobility (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Weimar, the German city of the grand duke’s court. The Gray Ghost comes from the coat and the silent stride.
Notable Weimaraners
Heidi, who lived in the Eisenhower White House. Man Ray and Fay Ray, stars of William Wegman’s photographs.
Good to Know
Needs hard exercise and constant company. Lonely Weimaraners turn destructive. The deep chest raises the risk of bloat.
Coats & Colors
A short, sleek coat in silver, mouse, or blue-gray. Eyes run amber, gray, or blue-gray.
By the Numbers
Fifty-five to ninety pounds. Bred in Germany in the early 1800s. Recognized by the AKC in 1943.
d: Ash lies with his chin on the dock plank. The lake can wait. So can he.
The Weimaraner started in Weimar, Germany, for the grand duke’s hunts.
Ghost points on the dune crest. Paw up, tail straight, the whole sky holding still.
Bandanas on, ears back, and the pontoon in no hurry. A fine Wednesday.
A bobber floats. A Weimaraner watches. Patience looks good in silver.
Weimaraner puppies are born with faint tiger stripes. They fade in days.
Puppies asleep in an overturned kayak. Sandy paws, pale blue eyes, no plans.
lw: The pier lights flick on, and the lake turns to pewter.

Ghost walks beside old Ash toward the little lighthouse. The young dog slows to the old dog’s pace. Silver coats, silver water. A Weimaraner is a ghost only to strangers. To its people it is the warmest thing on the pier.

p: A face full of wrinkles and a heart full of mischief.
s: The Pug looks worried. The Pug is not worried. The Pug is waiting for you to notice it is adorable.

The breed is ancient. Pugs lived in China more than two thousand years ago, where emperors kept them as palace companions. Traders carried them to Holland in the 1500s, and the Pug became a favorite of European courts.
Dutch legend says a Pug named Pompey barked a warning when Spanish soldiers crept toward the Prince of Orange in 1572. The prince lived. The Pug became a hero.
The breed motto is multum in parvo. Much in little. Josephine, wife of Napoleon, kept a Pug named Fortune. Queen Victoria loved them too. The AKC recognized the breed in 1885.
At home, a Pug snores, snorts, and shadows you from room to room. It hogs the couch and the covers. It eats anything and then looks at you for more.
Keep it cool, keep it trim, and expect a lap that is never empty. A group of Pugs is called a grumble. It is the best kind of noise.
rc: Much dog in a small package (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
No one knows for sure. One theory is the Latin pugnus, a fist, for the shape of the face.
Notable Pugs
Pompey, who saved a Dutch prince. Fortune, Josephine Bonaparte’s feisty Pug. Frank, the wisecracking Pug of Men in Black.
Good to Know
Short noses mean noisy breathing and trouble in heat. Watch the weight. Clean the wrinkles daily.
Coats & Colors
A short, smooth coat in fawn or black. The tail curls tight over the hip. The wrinkles are the trademark.
By the Numbers
Fourteen to eighteen pounds. Bred in China over two thousand years ago. Recognized by the AKC in 1885.
d: Old Winston naps on a hay bale in the fair barn, under a patchwork quilt.
The Pug’s motto is multum in parvo. Much in little. Look at that face.
Legend says Pompey the Pug saved a Dutch prince in 1572.
A Pug at an ice cream stand does not beg. He simply stares until it melts.
Meet the baby goat nose to nose. Both of you are startled. Both are fine.
A group of Pugs is called a grumble. Powdered sugar optional.
Old Winston sleeps on the grandstand bench. The lemonade waits beside him.
lw: The Ferris wheel glows, and the midway goes quiet.
Mugsy and Pearl head for the gate. She carries a stuffed prize bigger than her head. He snorts. Neither will explain. Pugs never do. The lights stay on behind them, and the grumble goes home.

p: A powder puff with a cheerful mind of its own.
s: The Bichon Frise looks like a cloud that learned to trot. It is white, round, and bouncy, and it acts as if every day is its birthday.
The breed comes from the Mediterranean. Sailors carried small white dogs from port to port, as pets and as trade goods. The dogs landed in Spain, Italy, and France.
The name is French. Bichon means little lapdog. Frisé means curly. Together they say curly lapdog, which is exactly right.

Kings loved them. In the 1500s, French nobles carried Bichons in baskets and dressed them in ribbons. After the French Revolution the dogs moved to the streets and the circus, and learned tricks to earn their supper. The AKC recognized the breed in 1972.
At home, a Bichon is a clown with perfect manners. It prances, it spins, and it greets every guest like a lost friend. It sheds little, but it needs a haircut every month.
Give it company, a brush, and a lap. A Bichon asks only to be in the middle of things, and it will brighten every room.
rc: A curly lapdog loved by kings (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Bichon is old French for little lapdog. Frisé means curly. The name describes the coat and the job.
Notable Bichons
Favorites of French kings and Spanish painters. Goya painted them. After the Revolution, Bichons became circus stars.
Good to Know
Sheds little, but the curly coat mats without brushing. Needs grooming every four to six weeks.
Coats & Colors
A plush, silky, curly coat. White, with cream or apricot shading allowed on a puppy.
By the Numbers
Twelve to eighteen pounds. Lives fourteen to fifteen years. Recognized by the AKC in 1972.
d: Cotton, thirteen years old, naps on the porch swing. She smells like lavender.
Bichon means little lapdog in French. Frisé means curly. The name is the dog.
King Henri III of France wore a basket of small dogs around his neck.
Two Bichons at the farm stand. The lavender lemonade is not for them.
Put your nose in the jar. Close your eyes. Let the bee wait.
Bichons once worked the circus, dancing on hind legs for supper.
Puppies asleep in a basket of cut lavender. The farm smells like a lullaby.
lw: The rows go violet, and the mountains turn blue.

Snowball walks the gravel path alone, a small white lantern between the rows. She stops. She sniffs. She trots on. A Bichon turns every path into a parade. Tonight the parade has one member, and she is plenty.

p: The African lion hound with a ridge of its own.
s: Look at the back of a Rhodesian Ridgeback. A strip of hair grows the wrong way, from the tail toward the shoulders. It is the ridge, and it defines the breed.
The story begins in southern Africa. European settlers brought hounds and guard dogs. They bred them with the half-wild, ridged dogs of the Khoikhoi people.

Hunters in Rhodesia used the dogs to track lions and hold them at bay until the hunter arrived. People called the breed the African Lion Hound. The dogs did not fight the lion. They kept it busy and kept clear.
In 1922, breeders in Bulawayo wrote the first standard. The AKC recognized the breed in 1955.
At home, a Ridgeback is calm indoors and a rocket outdoors. It is dignified, loyal, and sometimes stubborn. It bonds with its family, and it keeps its opinion of strangers private.
Give it miles to run and a firm, kind leader. It will give you a lifetime of quiet company.
rc: Africa’s lion hound, ridge and all (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Rhodesian for the African region where the breed was standardized. Ridgeback for the stripe of hair along its spine.
Notable Ridgebacks
Few are famous by name. The breed is the legend, bred to hold lions at bay across the African bush.
Good to Know
Strong, smart, and independent. Needs steady training and daily running. Ask breeders about dermoid sinus, a skin defect.
Coats & Colors
A short, sleek coat in light to red wheaten. The ridge forms two matching crowns. A dark mask is common.
By the Numbers
Seventy to eighty-five pounds. Standard written in 1922. Recognized by the AKC in 1955.
d: Old Jabari rests in the rock shade. The desert can do its worst. He is not moving.
The ridge grows backward along the spine. Every Ridgeback has one.
Ridgebacks held lions at bay in Africa. A thunderhead is nothing.
Two Ridgebacks climb the canyon trail. The cliffs are not impressed.
A horned lizard holds still. So does Zuri. Respect looks like patience.
A show ridge needs two matching whorls, called crowns. Dust is optional.
Puppies sleep against old Jabari by lantern light. He has seen many deserts.
lw: The sky goes plum, and the saguaros stand like sentries.
Kofi and Zuri walk the dusty road home. Their coats match the dust, and their ridges catch the last light. A Ridgeback is a lion hound by trade and a house cat by evening. The lantern is lit at camp.

p: A nose with legs, and ears that arrive first.
s: A Basset Hound is mostly nose, ears, and sorrow. It is also mostly joy. It simply hides it under a lot of skin.
The breed began in France. Bas means low in French. Monks and nobles bred short-legged hounds from the old St. Hubert hounds, so hunters on foot could keep up.

A Basset’s nose is second only to the Bloodhound’s. Many people believe the long ears sweep scent toward the nose, and the loose skin holds it there. Every part is built for one job, following a trail.
