The Basset came to America in the 1800s, and the AKC recognized it in 1885. Then television and one famous shoe company made it a star.
At home, a Basset is slow, loyal, and stubborn. It will follow its nose past your call, then give you the look that says it did not hear. It loves children, naps, and food, in any order.
Keep it lean, keep the ears clean, and skip the stairs. A Basset needs a gentle leader and an unhurried walk.
rc: A low hound with a legendary nose (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Bas is French for low. A Basset is a low hound, bred to hunt close to the ground.
Notable Bassets
Flash, Rosco’s sidekick on The Dukes of Hazzard. The Hush Puppies shoe mascot, the best-known Basset of all.
Good to Know
The long back needs support, so skip jumps and stairs. Ears need regular cleaning. Easy to overfeed.
Coats & Colors
A short, smooth coat in tricolor or lemon and white. Loose skin, and ears that reach the floor.
By the Numbers
Forty to sixty-five pounds. Eleven to fifteen inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1885.
d: Old Gumbo naps on the porch. The ceiling fan turns. Nothing is urgent.
Bas means low in French. Beignet is proof, loping low down the levee.
Old French monastery hounds are the Basset’s family tree. Boudreaux drifts on.
Chins on the cooler lid. Eyes on the cane pole. Patience is a Basset art.
A crawfish raises its claws. Beignet reconsiders. Wise dogs know when to back up.
A Basset’s nose is second only to the Bloodhound’s. Ears are optional.
Puppies on a porch quilt. Their ears are tangled. Nobody is in a hurry.
lw: The fireflies rise, and the bayou goes gold.

Boudreaux walks the gravel road beside old Gumbo. The young dog slows down. The old dog slows more. A rocking chair glows on the porch ahead. A Basset knows where home is. It follows its nose there every night.

p: The smallest dog with the biggest opinions.
s: The Chihuahua is the smallest dog breed in the world. It has never accepted this.

The breed is named for the Mexican state of Chihuahua, where Americans found these little dogs in the 1800s. Likely ancestors are the Techichi, a small dog kept by the Toltec people and later by the Aztecs.
Pottery and carvings from ancient Mexico show small dogs much like today’s. The Chihuahua is an old soul in a tiny coat.
The AKC recognized the breed in 1904. Then ads made it a star. A Chihuahua named Gidget sold tacos on television in the late 1990s and made the breed a household name.
Two coats exist, smooth and long. Both have the same spirit. A Chihuahua trembles when cold and barks when bored. It picks one person and guards them with its whole body.
Keep it warm, keep it safe from big dogs, and keep the treats small. It can live up to sixteen years. That is a long time to be in charge.
rc: The world’s smallest breed (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Chihuahua, the Mexican state where Americans found the breed in the 1800s.
Notable Chihuahuas
Gidget, the Taco Bell dog of the late 1990s. Bruiser, Elle Woods’s loyal companion in Legally Blonde.
Good to Know
Small and fragile, so handle with care. Feels the cold. Needs early socializing and dental care.
Coats & Colors
Smooth or long coat, in nearly every color and pattern. Ears stand tall. The tail curves over the back.
By the Numbers
Under six pounds. Five to eight inches tall. Lives fourteen to sixteen years. Recognized by the AKC in 1904.
d: Chato, fourteen years old, naps in the sunny window niche. He earned the sun.
The Chihuahua is the smallest breed in the world. It does not know that.
Paco rules the roof. One small dog, one enormous New Mexico sky.
A smooth coat and a long coat share a basket. Same breed, different hair.
Red chile makes the eyes water. Luz sniffs anyway. Curious beats comfortable.
Chihuahua puppies are born with a soft spot on the skull. It closes with age.
Puppies asleep in a terracotta pot. The marigolds look jealous.
lw: The patio lights come on, and the adobe glows.

Paco trots the wall at dusk, ears tall, tail up. He checks the lights. He checks the sky. Then he heads for the warm door. Chihuahuas are small enough to be carried. They prefer to walk, and they prefer to lead.

p: A pocket-size herder with a big engine.
s: The Miniature American Shepherd packs a full herding dog into a smaller coat. It has the Aussie brain, the Aussie energy, and the Aussie opinions. Only the size is different.

Breeders in California started the breed in the 1960s. They selected small Australian Shepherds, and the little dogs won over rodeo fans and horse owners. They fit in a truck cab and still did a full day’s work.
The breed first went by Miniature Australian Shepherd. The name changed to Miniature American Shepherd, and the AKC recognized it in 2015.
Minis herd, perform tricks, and visit hospitals. Their coats come in black, red, blue merle, and red merle, with or without white and copper trim.
At home, they are fast, funny, and always watching. A Mini will herd your kids, your cat, and your guests. It learns a trick in five tries and asks for another.
Give it a trail, a task, and a campsite, and it will be the best traveler you know. It loves the ride as much as the arrival.
rc: A pocket herder bred in California (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Miniature for the size. American because the breed was built in the United States.
Notable Minis
Rodeo and horse-show trick dogs made the breed famous. Today they star in agility rings and on trail packs.
Good to Know
Brilliant and busy, so it needs daily jobs. Breeders avoid merle-to-merle pairings, which risk blindness and deafness.
Coats & Colors
A medium double coat in black, red, blue merle, or red merle, with white, copper, or both.
By the Numbers
Twenty to forty pounds. Thirteen to eighteen inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 2015.
d: Old Rusty snoozes in the tent. Dawn glows through the walls. He is in no rush.
Mini American Shepherds were bred in California in the 1960s.
Nacho stands on the dome. Granite below, sky above. Small and unafraid.
Two dogs, a cooler, a guitar, and the open road. Everything a trip needs.
National Dog Day. Skye celebrates by inspecting a marshmallow.
Roll in the pine needles. Come home with souvenirs. That is a real trip.
Puppies on a flannel bag beside empty hiking boots. They will grow into them.
lw: The fire ring glows, and the pines go dark.

Nacho and Skye walk the edge of camp as the smoke climbs. Embers pop. Stars come out over the granite. A Mini Aussie never really goes off duty. It checks the fire, it checks the camp, and then it sleeps beside you.

p: A little lion with a flower for a face.
s: Shih Tzu means lion in Chinese. The Shih Tzu does not roar. It trots, it tosses its topknot, and it accepts your devotion.

The breed has roots in Tibet and China, where small, long-haired dogs were prized by the imperial court. Chinese emperors kept them as palace companions, and the Dowager Empress Cixi was a famous fan in the late 1800s.
Legend says Buddha traveled with a small dog that could turn into a lion to protect him. Chinese artists carved lion-dogs in jade and stone. The Shih Tzu is the living version.
British officers brought a few dogs home in the 1930s. After World War II, American soldiers brought more. The AKC recognized the breed in 1969.
At home, a Shih Tzu has one job, which is to be adored. It has a flat, friendly face, a plume of a tail, and a sunny opinion of strangers.
Brush it daily, keep its eyes clean, and mind the heat. A Shih Tzu thrives on love and a short walk. Be ready to carry it home.
rc: The little lion of the Chinese court (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Shih Tzu means lion in Chinese. The long mane and bold walk earned the name.
Notable Shih Tzus
Palace pets of Chinese emperors. Dowager Empress Cixi kept and loved them in the late 1800s.
Good to Know
Flat faces overheat, so keep it cool. Eyes need daily wipes and the coat needs brushing. Many owners clip it short.
Coats & Colors
A long, flowing double coat in gold, black, liver, white, or mixed. The tail curls over the back like a plume.
By the Numbers
Nine to sixteen pounds. Nine to ten and a half inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1969.
d: Old Oscar sleeps in the beach tote. The tide is coming. He will not notice.
Shih Tzu means lion in Chinese. Zeus runs the boardwalk like a king.
Legend says Buddha’s little dog could turn into a lion. Mei Mei is practicing.
Two Shih Tzus, one soft-serve cone, zero patience. The bench is a battlefield.
Zeus listens to the shell. The sea has plenty to say. Slow down and hear it.
The ribbon topknot keeps hair out of the eyes. In sea wind, it loses.
Puppies ride the beach wagon. Towels, flip-flops, and the best seat in town.
lw: The neon wakes, and the wet planks glow.

Mei Mei walks the boardwalk as the lights come on. Her topknot is crooked. Her tail is high. Pink and blue light spills across the boards. Summer is nearly over. A Shih Tzu does not mind. It walks like a small lion who owns the place.

p: The elegant guardian with a tender streak.
s: The Doberman Pinscher looks like a statue and acts like a shadow. Every muscle is polished. Every glance is on you.
Louis Dobermann, a tax collector in Apolda, Germany, created the breed in the 1890s. He wanted a loyal, fearless dog to walk beside him on his rounds. The exact recipe was never written down.
The result was fast, strong, and smart. After Dobermann died in 1894, breeders refined the dog into the sleek athlete we know. The AKC recognized the breed in 1908.
In World War II, the U.S. Marines used Dobermans as scouts and messengers in the Pacific, most famously on Guam in 1944. A war dog memorial there honors the dogs that died.
At home, a Doberman is not the villain of the movies. It is affectionate, eager, and clingy. It leans on you, stares at you, and waits for the next job.
Give it training, exercise, and respect, and it will protect you for life. Even in a pool noodle, it keeps its dignity.
rc: A tax collector’s loyal bodyguard (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Louis Dobermann, the German tax collector who created the breed. Pinscher is German for a terrier type.
Notable Dobermans
Kurt, a Marine war dog honored on Guam. Dobermans also serve as police and search dogs.
Good to Know
Heart disease occurs, so choose a screened breeder. Needs daily exercise and steady training. Hates being left alone.
Coats & Colors
A short, sleek coat in black, red, blue, or fawn, with rust markings.
By the Numbers
Sixty to one hundred pounds. Created in the 1890s. Recognized by the AKC in 1908.
d: Labor Day weekend. Duchess claims the chair and the quilt.
Labor Day. The breed’s creator was a tax collector, so he knew all about work.
Louis Dobermann wanted a loyal dog for his rounds. Titan guards the vineyard.
Two Dobermans, two burgers, one rule. Wait for the word.
A dragonfly lands on the post. Ruby holds still. Gentle is a kind of strength.
Dobermans cling to their people. Titan wears the noodle with dignity.
Puppies in a rope hammock. Two trees, one summer, and no place to be.
lw: The lake turns copper, and the last light of summer fades.

Titan walks the lakeside road with old Duchess. He matches her pace. She leans, just a little, on his shoulder. A Doberman is a guardian all day. At dusk it is a friend. The first leaf drops, and neither dog looks up.

p: The bird dog with boundless spring in its step.
s: The Brittany is a small hunter with a big motor. It is compact, quick, and always ready for the next field.

The breed comes from Brittany, a province in northwest France. Hunters there kept bright orange and white dogs that could find birds and point them. Paintings and tapestries from the 1600s show similar dogs.
The Brittany is a spaniel that points, like a setter. It works close, it retrieves, and it never seems to tire. The AKC recognized the breed in 1934. In 1982 it dropped Spaniel from the name.
Many Brittanys are born with short tails, or none at all. Breeders call it a natural bobtail. Short tail or long, the whole back end wags.
At home, a Brittany is sweet, sensitive, and always in motion. It loves its people with its whole body. It wants a trail, a mission, and dinner at the end.
Give it a mountain and a good pair of boots, and it will take you to the top and then ask what is next.
rc: France’s pointing spaniel (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Brittany, the province in northwest France. The AKC dropped Spaniel from the name in 1982.
Notable Brittanys
Few are famous by name. The breed is the star, a spaniel that points like a setter and a field favorite since the 1930s.
Good to Know
Needs hard daily exercise or it turns restless. Sensitive to harsh words. Ask breeders about hips.
Coats & Colors
A dense, flat or wavy coat in orange and white or liver and white, often ticked. The tail is short or docked.
By the Numbers
Thirty to forty pounds. Seventeen and a half to twenty and a half inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1934.
d: Old Jasper wakes by the tent. Dew on the grass. The mountains can wait.
Brittany is a province in France. The dog is a spaniel that points.
Tango points in the goldenrod. One paw up, sun low, the whole field still.
Mount Washington boasts the world’s worst weather. Today is perfect.
Woolly bear caterpillars predict winter, folks say. Maple takes no chances.
Many Brittanys are born with short tails. They wag from the shoulders back.
Puppies asleep in the hiking pack beside the thermos. The trail can wait.
lw: The ridges stack in blue, and a lodge light glows far below.

Tango and Maple walk the trail down at dusk. The day’s miles are in their legs. Maple walks a few steps ahead, then waits. Leaves are turning at the edges. A Brittany ends the day tired and happy, and it already asks about tomorrow.

p: A small herder with a big voice and bigger heart.
s: The Shetland Sheepdog looks like a Collie that shrank in the wash. It did not. It was built small on purpose, and it works as hard as any dog twice its size.

The breed comes from the Shetland Islands, off the north coast of Scotland. Crofters farmed thin soil and kept small animals, so they kept small dogs. A Sheltie herded sheep and ponies and barked at anything that wandered off.
Early on, the breed was called the Shetland Collie. Collie breeders objected, and the name changed. The AKC recognized the Shetland Sheepdog in 1911.
Shelties still herd, but most now herd families. They are quick learners and star in agility and obedience rings. They watch your face, read your mood, and answer almost before you ask.
At home, a Sheltie is gentle, sensitive, and talkative. It will bark at the mailman, the wind, and a falling leaf. It will also sit beside you through every bad day.
Give it a job, a brush, and a quiet voice. A Sheltie asks for little, and it gives back everything.
rc: A small herder from the Scottish isles (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Shetland for the Scottish islands. The early name, Shetland Collie, was dropped after Collie breeders objected.
Notable Shelties
Few are famous by name. The breed is the star, a perennial winner in agility and obedience rings.
Good to Know
Sensitive and vocal. Needs early training to manage the barking. The thick double coat sheds, and needs brushing.
Coats & Colors
A long, harsh outer coat over a soft undercoat, with a full ruff. Sable, tricolor, or blue merle, with white.
By the Numbers
Fourteen to twenty-seven pounds. Thirteen to sixteen inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1911.
d: Old Sparky naps on the porch glider with a plaid blanket and warm cider close by.
The Sheltie began on the Shetland Islands, herding sheep and ponies.
Misty stands above the orchard. The valley is gold. The whole flock is accounted for.
Shelties were once called Shetland Collies. Collie breeders said no.
Autumn begins today. Merlin paws a bobbing apple. Patience wins the apple.
An apple clamped in her jaws and an innocent look. Misty denies everything.
Puppies asleep in an apple crate lined with flannel. Orchard dreams.
lw: The shadows lengthen, and the rows glow gold.
Misty and old Sparky walk the dirt road at dusk. Apple trees line both sides. She keeps to his slow pace. A Sheltie herds by instinct. Tonight the only flock is two dogs, and the only job is home.

p: A tireless field dog that never met a cornfield it didn’t love.
s: A German Shorthaired Pointer does not rest. It scans, it sniffs, and it waits for the word. Then it is gone across the field like a liver-colored arrow.

The breed began in Germany in the 1800s. Hunters wanted one dog that could do everything. It had to point, track, retrieve, and swim, in fields, woods, and water. German breeders crossed pointers with hounds and bird dogs until they had it.
The dog arrived in America in the 1920s and the AKC recognized it in 1930. It took to American fields at once.
A GSP has a water-friendly coat and webbed feet. It hunts upland birds in the morning and retrieves ducks from cold water in the afternoon. Few breeds do both so well.
At home, a GSP is affectionate, goofy, and exhausting. It needs miles of running every day. Without them, it will rearrange your furniture. With them, it is a gentle shadow.
Give it a field, a job, and a family. In 2016, one named CJ won Best in Show at Westminster.
rc: Germany’s do-everything bird dog (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
German for the country. Shorthaired for the coat. Pointer for the way the dog freezes on a scent.
Notable GSPs
CJ, the 2016 Westminster Best in Show winner. Many GSPs also work as search dogs and bird hunting partners.
Good to Know
Needs hard daily exercise and a job. Bored GSPs turn destructive. Ask breeders about hips and bloat.
Coats & Colors
A short, dense, water-resistant coat in liver or black, solid or with white, often ticked or roan.
By the Numbers
Forty-five to seventy pounds. Twenty-one to twenty-five inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1930.
d: Old Rusty sleeps on the tailgate under a wool blanket. Frost on the field.
German hunters wanted one dog to point, track, retrieve, and swim.
Ranger points at the field’s edge. One paw up. The whole cornfield holds its breath.
Two pointers on a hay stack, noses to the wind. The farm is an open book.
A caterpillar crosses the road. Annie stops. A good pointer respects a crossing.
In 2016, CJ, a GSP, won Best in Show at Westminster.
Puppies asleep on an old flannel jacket in the pickup. Field dreams.
lw: The farm road turns bronze, and the corn rustles.
Ranger and Annie walk home between the rows. Their coats match the stalks. The long shadows lead the way. A GSP is a hunter by trade. At dusk it is just tired and happy, and the pickup is warm.

p: A small white terrier with a big opinion of itself.
s: The West Highland White Terrier is the size of a loaf of bread and the attitude of a mountain. It carries itself like a general and digs like a gold miner.
The breed comes from the West Highlands of Scotland. Farmers kept sturdy little terriers to hunt rats, foxes, and badgers among the rocks. The best ones worked underground, and they needed courage.

A famous story says Colonel Malcolm of Poltalloch mistook one of his red terriers for a fox and shot it by accident. He then bred white dogs so nobody would make the mistake again. Whether true or not, the dogs stayed white.
The AKC recognized the breed in 1908. Today the Westie is a TV star, a dog food mascot, and one of the best-loved small dogs in America.
At home, a Westie is bold, cheerful, and busy. It digs, it barks, and it assumes the household needs its supervision. It will play fetch until you drop.
Give it a fenced yard, a brush, and a sense of humor. A Westie will supply the rest.
rc: The small white terrier of Scotland (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for the West Highlands of Scotland. The earlier name was the Poltalloch Terrier, after the Malcolm family estate.
Notable Westies
Cesar, the dog food mascot. A Westie also trots across the label of a famous Scotch whisky.
Good to Know
Digs, barks, and chases. Skin allergies are common. A hand-stripped coat keeps the texture right.
Coats & Colors
A harsh white outer coat over a soft undercoat. Black nose, dark eyes, and a carrot-shaped tail.
By the Numbers
Fifteen to twenty pounds. Ten to eleven inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1908.
d: Old Mac naps on a tartan blanket by the stove. The embers keep watch.
World Animal Day. The Westie began as a Scottish rat catcher in the rocks.
A Scottish colonel bred white terriers so he would never mistake one for a fox.
Two Westies ride a wagon full of pumpkins. They think they are the harvest.
A Highland cow looms over Poppy. She does not blink. Meet the world head on.
A muddy nose tells the whole story. Angus denies everything.
Puppies tumble in the leaves. No rules apply.
lw: The jack-o’-lanterns flicker, and the sky goes violet.
Angus and Poppy leave the glowing patch together. Their white coats catch every ember of light. A Westie leaves a party only when it has seen all of it. Tonight, they have seen enough.

p: A gentle giant with a gamekeeper’s past.
s: The Bullmastiff looks like a bouncer and acts like a pillow. It weighs as much as a grown man, and it would love to sit in your lap.

The breed began in England in the 1800s. Landowners hired gamekeepers to protect their estates from poachers. The gamekeepers needed a dog that could run, tackle, and hold a trespasser without biting. So they crossed the Mastiff for size with the Bulldog for courage.
The result was the Gamekeeper’s Night Dog. It was quiet, brave, and calm. The AKC recognized the Bullmastiff in 1934.
Today the job is easier. A Bullmastiff guards the house by existing. It lies in the doorway, snores, and lets its size do the talking.
At home, it is gentle, loyal, and drooly. It loves its family, tolerates visitors, and needs only a short walk and a long nap.
Give it shade, a soft bed, and a towel for the jowls. A Bullmastiff will guard you for life, and it will drool on you the whole time.
rc: The gamekeeper’s gentle night dog (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
A blend of the two parent breeds, the Bulldog and the Mastiff.
Notable Bullmastiffs
Butkus, Sylvester Stallone’s own dog and the loyal companion in the first Rocky film.
Good to Know
Drools, snores, and sheds. Overheats easily. A deep chest raises the risk of bloat. Lifespans are short.
Coats & Colors
A short, dense coat in fawn, red, or brindle. A black mask is the standard.
By the Numbers
One hundred to one hundred thirty pounds. Created in England in the 1800s. Recognized by the AKC in 1934.
d: Old Gus naps on the porch beside the pumpkins. The rocking chair rocks.
A holiday for people. For a Bullmastiff, every day is for sitting.
English gamekeepers bred this dog to hold poachers without biting.
Two giants on the village green. The cider stand is on high alert.
A chipmunk on the wall. Bella blinks. Small things deserve respect.
Butkus, Stallone’s Bullmastiff, played Rocky’s dog. No stunt double needed.
Puppies asleep in a raked pile of leaves, only their noses showing.
lw: The maples glow, and the jack-o’-lanterns flicker.

Bruno and old Gus walk the village street at dusk. The older dog sets the pace, and the younger one matches it. Porch lights come on, one by one. A Bullmastiff needs little. A slow walk home is plenty.

p: The working dog that never clocks out.
s: A Belgian Malinois is a coiled spring in a fawn coat. It sits quietly, watches everything, and is ready to run before you finish the word.

The breed comes from Belgium. In the 1890s, breeders in and around the city of Malines selected herding dogs for brains and drive. Four Belgian sheepdog varieties came out of that effort. The Malinois is the short-haired fawn one.
The AKC recognized the breed in 1959. Since then, it has won a reputation as one of the best working dogs in the world.
Malinois work as police dogs, military dogs, and search dogs. A Malinois named Cairo served on the 2011 raid that found Osama bin Laden. Secret Service Malinois guard the White House grounds.
At home, it is not a casual pet. It needs a purpose, miles of exercise, and an owner who understands dogs. Bored Malinois dismantle houses.
Give it a trail, a task, and a fair leader. A Malinois will give you the most focused partnership of your life.
rc: The elite working dog from Belgium (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Malinois is French for from Malines, the Belgian city now called Mechelen.
Notable Malinois
Cairo, the Navy SEAL dog who took part in the 2011 raid on Osama bin Laden. Secret Service Malinois guard the White House.
Good to Know
Needs hard work, training, and exercise every day. Not a beginner’s dog. Bored Malinois can be destructive.
Coats & Colors
A short, weather-resistant coat in rich fawn to mahogany, with a black mask and black ears.
By the Numbers
Forty to eighty pounds. Twenty-two to twenty-six inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1959.
d: Old Hunter rests on a creek rock at dawn. Mist rises. He has seen many mornings.
Named for Malines, a Belgian city. One of four Belgian sheepdog types.
Cairo, a Malinois, served on the 2011 raid that found bin Laden.
Two Malinois lead the way up the switchbacks. The mountain was not a question.
A stick bobs in the eddy. Sable watches, paw raised. Patience is also a job.
A stick twice his length. Maverick will fit it through the trees. Eventually.
Puppies on a mossy log in a bed of fall leaves. They are already in charge.
lw: The mountain fog turns blue, and the road goes quiet.
Maverick and Sable walk the gravel road between bare trees. The work is done. For once, they stroll. A Malinois always listens, even in sleep. Tonight, the only thing to hear is the creek.

p: The American Gentleman in a tuxedo coat.
s: The Boston Terrier looks ready for a formal dinner. Black and white coat, big round eyes, and a manner that says it will be seated now.

The breed was born in Boston in the 1870s. A local man named Robert Hooper owned a dog called Judge, a mix of an English Bulldog and a white English Terrier. Judge is the father of nearly every Boston Terrier that followed.
Boston breeders refined the line into a smaller, smoother dog. The AKC recognized the breed in 1893. It was one of the first American breeds on the list. Massachusetts made it the state dog.
The Boston Terrier is a true American original. People called it the American Gentleman, for its tuxedo markings and polite ways.
At home, a Boston is cheerful, clownish, and affectionate. It snorts, it snores, and it wants to be in the middle of the action. College towns love them.
Keep it cool, keep it close, and let it supervise your Saturday. A Boston Terrier makes any game better.
rc: Boston’s own tuxedo gentleman (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Boston, Massachusetts, where the breed began. Early fans called it the Round Head, then the Bullet Head.
Notable Boston Terriers
Judge, the founding sire of the breed. Rhett, the live mascot of Boston University.
Good to Know
A short nose means noisy breathing and trouble in heat. Eyes need care. Good with children and quick to learn.
Coats & Colors
A short, smooth coat in black, brindle, or seal, with white markings. The tuxedo look is the standard.
By the Numbers
Twelve to twenty-five pounds. Fifteen to seventeen inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1893.
d: Old Gus naps on a stack of sweaters in the window seat. Peak foliage can wait.
The Boston Terrier began in Boston in the 1870s. Massachusetts made it the state dog.
Robert Hooper’s dog Judge founded the breed. Nearly every Boston descends from him.
Two Bostons at a tailgate, noses up. Football is the second attraction.
A squirrel by the lamp post. Molly holds still. Stare long enough and anything blinks.
A tiny football helmet is a lot to ask. Rhett has agreed to it for the photo.
Old Gus naps on a stadium blanket. The score is irrelevant.
lw: The brick halls glow, and the leaf piles go gold.
Rhett and Molly cross the campus lawn at dusk. The windows are lit. The game is over. A Boston Terrier never wins or loses. It just goes home, tuxedo and all, and falls asleep before dessert.

p: The comedian in bat ears, now America’s favorite.
s: The French Bulldog has bat ears, a squashed face, and the confidence of a movie star. It snores, it snorts, and it has taken over the country.

The breed began in England. Lace makers in Nottingham bred small Bulldogs as lap companions. When the lace trade moved to France in the 1800s, the workers took their little dogs along. French breeders loved them and favored the upright bat ears.
The Frenchie became a Parisian fashion in the late 1800s. Americans imported it, and the AKC recognized the breed in 1898. A Frenchie even sailed on the Titanic.
For more than a century it stayed a cult favorite. Then, in 2022, it passed the Labrador to become America’s No. 1 breed. It has held the top spot every year since, through 2025.
At home, a Frenchie is a clown, a snuggler, and a lap warmer. It does not need much exercise. It needs company, a cool room, and a comfy couch.
Mind the heat, mind the breathing, and expect an audience wherever you go. A Frenchie always has an opinion.
rc: No. 1 in America four years running (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
French because the breed took shape in France. English lace workers brought the little Bulldogs across the Channel.
Notable Frenchies
Gamin de Pycombe, a Frenchie aboard the Titanic. Koji and Gustav, Lady Gaga’s famous pair.
Good to Know
A short nose means noisy breathing and trouble in heat. Many cannot swim well. Choose a health-tested breeder.
Coats & Colors
A short, smooth coat in brindle, fawn, cream, or pied. Bat ears stand tall.
By the Numbers
Under twenty-eight pounds. Eleven to thirteen inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1898. No. 1 since 2022.
d: Halloween. Old Pierre sleeps in a pumpkin bed in a witch hat. He earned it.
Nottingham lace workers bred the first Frenchies. They took them to France.
A Frenchie named Gamin de Pycombe sailed on the Titanic in 1912.
Two Frenchies, matching costumes, one candy bucket. The math is not in their favor.
A plastic skeleton on the stoop. Colette sniffs. Fear is only a stranger.
A lion mane on a Frenchie. Gaston says he was not consulted.
Puppies asleep in a trick-or-treat bucket. Candy wrappers all around.
lw: The jack-o’-lanterns flicker, and the street goes quiet.
Gaston and Colette walk the block at twilight. Orange light spills across the stoops. Their bat ears catch every sound. A Frenchie loves a parade, and tonight the whole street is one.

p: Calm strength with a soft spot for its people.
s: The Rottweiler looks serious. It is serious. It is also a mush when it comes to its family, and a clown when no one is looking.

The breed takes its name from Rottweil, a town in southern Germany. The story goes that the dogs descend from the drover dogs of the Roman legions, who marched over the Alps with cattle. After the Romans left, the dogs stayed.
For centuries, butchers in Rottweil used them to drive cattle to market. Butchers are said to have hung the money pouch around the dog’s neck on the way home. Few thieves tried to take it.

By the 1900s, the Rottweiler had become a police dog and war dog, and the AKC recognized it in 1931. Rottweilers served as messengers and guards in wartime, and they still work as police, search, and service dogs.
At home, a Rottweiler is calm, loyal, and watchful. It bonds hard to its family. It needs training, firm and kind, and regular exercise.
Give it a job and a place by your side. A Rottweiler will guard you without needing to be told.
rc: The butcher’s dog of Rottweil (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Rottweil, the German market town where butchers kept the breed.
Notable Rottweilers
Few are famous by name. The breed is celebrated for police, search, and guide work.
Good to Know
Needs training and early socializing. Strong and heavy, so an owner must be firm and kind. Screen hips and elbows.
Coats & Colors
A short, dense black coat with rust to mahogany markings. The tail is docked or natural.
By the Numbers
Eighty to one hundred thirty-five pounds. Twenty-two to twenty-seven inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1931.
d: Daylight saving ends. Hank slept through the extra hour. Lucky dog.
The Rottweiler is named for Rottweil, a German town, where butchers kept the breed.
Roman legions drove cattle over the Alps. Rottweilers descend from their dogs.
Flags line the street. Two Rottweilers sit at the curb by a veteran’s cap and flag.
Veterans Day. Greta sniffs a red leaf. Gentle is a kind of strength.
Rottweilers served as messengers and guards in wartime. Axel holds the flag gently.
Puppies asleep on a folded flannel jacket on the porch chair. All is well.
lw: The maples stand bare, and the street is still.
Axel and Greta walk home at dusk. The flags are down. Their steps match. A Rottweiler never really goes off duty. Tonight the duty is simple. Walk the street, look both ways, and bring everyone home.

p: A bearded little farm dog with a big personality.
s: The Miniature Schnauzer has a beard, eyebrows, and a look that says it has already read your mail. It is small, sharp, and never dull.

The breed comes from Germany in the 1800s. Farmers wanted a small ratter to keep barns and stables clear. They crossed small Standard Schnauzers with other small breeds, like the Affenpinscher, until they had a bright, bold terrier type in a compact frame.
Schnauzer comes from the German word for snout. The first one was shown in Germany in 1899. The AKC recognized the breed in 1926.
It is the only Schnauzer in the Terrier group. It has the terrier spirit, but a gentler heart, and it has long been one of America’s favorite small dogs.
At home, a Miniature Schnauzer is alert, cheerful, and chatty. It barks at visitors and then loves them. It likes games, walks, and a place on the couch.
Groom the beard and brush the coat. Give it daily exercise and a good joke. A Schnauzer will keep up its end.
rc: A bearded ratter turned family pet (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Schnauzer is German for snout. The name celebrates the bristly muzzle.
Notable Miniature Schnauzers
Few are famous by name. The breed is a family favorite, and a regular in American show rings.
Good to Know
Barks, and sheds little. The coat needs grooming every six weeks. Prone to pancreatitis on fatty foods.
Coats & Colors
A wiry outer coat over a soft undercoat. Salt and pepper, black and silver, or solid black.
By the Numbers
Eleven to twenty pounds. Twelve to fourteen inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1926.
d: Old Max naps in a basket of flannels on the porch swing. The leaves can wait.
Schnauzer is German for snout. The beard is the family trademark.
German farmers bred small ratters for the barn. The Schnauzer got the job.
Two Schnauzers, one rake, one pile of leaves. Heads tilt in perfect unison.
An acorn on the ground. Greta sniffs. Small things are worth a good look.
A leaf in the beard, a twig in the ear. Otis will not be told.
Puppies asleep in a wheelbarrow of leaves. The harvest is complete.
lw: The windows glow, and the leaf piles line the walk.

Otis and Greta stroll down the suburban sidewalk. Dinner is cooking behind every curtain. A Schnauzer reads the evening like a newspaper. Tonight the headline is calm, and every dog in the block agrees.

p: The biggest heart in the biggest body.
s: The Mastiff is huge, and it is gentle. It can stand on its hind legs and look you in the eye. It would much prefer to lie down.

The breed is ancient. Large guard dogs existed in Britain when the Romans arrived, and the Mastiff descends from them. For centuries, they guarded estates and fought in the arena, and later they guarded homes.
After World War II, the breed in England nearly disappeared. American and Canadian Mastiffs helped bring it back. The AKC recognized the breed in 1885.
An English Mastiff named Aicama Zorba earned a Guinness record in the late 1980s as the heaviest dog ever, at 343 pounds. That is more than most grown men.
At home, a Mastiff is calm, loyal, and slow. It drools, it snores, and it leans its full weight on you. It guards through sheer presence.
Give it a big bed, a big yard, and a huge towel. A Mastiff is a thankful guest at any Thanksgiving table.
rc: The oldest giant, still gentle (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Probably from an old French word meaning tamed. The Mastiff was the tamed guardian of the estate.
Notable Mastiffs
Aicama Zorba, the Guinness record holder at 343 pounds, in 1989.
Good to Know
Drools, snores, and overheats. Prone to bloat, so feed small meals. Giant breeds have shorter lives.
Coats & Colors
A short, dense coat in fawn, apricot, or brindle. A black mask and ears are the standard.
By the Numbers
One hundred twenty to two hundred thirty pounds. Recognized by the AKC in 1885. Britain’s oldest giant.
d: Old Titus sleeps in the hall on a braided rug. A pushed-back chair beside him.
Mastiffs have guarded British estates for about two thousand years.
After World War II, American dogs helped save the nearly lost English Mastiff.
Two Mastiffs rest their chins on the Thanksgiving table. Their eyes follow the turkey.
Thanksgiving. A pie on the sill. Honey closes her eyes. Gratitude takes many forms.
A dinner roll on a Mastiff’s nose. Dignity intact. Dinner will be served.
Old Titus sleeps under the table among empty chairs. All have been fed.
lw: The windows glow, and the cold sets in.
Atlas and Honey walk the country road after dinner. They are full and slow. Their breath makes small clouds. A Mastiff has no need to hurry. The farmhouse is behind them, and the evening is long.

p: A tiny terrier with a heart too big for its body.
s: The Yorkshire Terrier weighs about as much as a bag of sugar. It carries itself like a lion tamer.

The breed began in northern England in the mid-1800s. Scottish weavers moved to Yorkshire to work in the mills and brought small terriers with them. The dogs caught rats in the mills and mines. They had to be fast, fearless, and small enough to go anywhere.
A dog named Huddersfield Ben, born in 1865, became the model for the breed. Breeders made the coat longer, silkier, and blue. The AKC recognized the Yorkie in 1885.
Yorkies are born black and tan. The color changes to steel blue and gold as they grow. Each coat is long enough to sweep the floor if you let it.
In World War II, a four-pound Yorkie named Smoky became a war hero in the Pacific. She pulled a telegraph wire through a narrow pipe and boosted the morale of her unit.
At home, a Yorkie is bold, devoted, and a little bossy. Give it a lap, a bow, and a small coat for winter.
rc: The mill town ratter turned lap favorite (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Yorkshire, the English county where mill workers developed the breed.
Notable Yorkies
Huddersfield Ben, the model sire of the breed. Smoky, the four-pound World War II hero.
Good to Know
Tiny and fragile. Feels the cold. Needs regular brushing and dental care. Quick to bark.
Coats & Colors
A long, silky coat in steel blue and tan. Puppies are born black and tan.
By the Numbers
Up to seven pounds. Seven to eight inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1885.
d: Old Peanut naps on a plaid blanket in the wagon. A fresh tree rides on the roof.
Yorkies are born black and tan. The steel blue comes later.
Smoky, a four-pound Yorkie, served in the Pacific in World War II.
Two Yorkies ride a red wagon beside a little cut tree. Smooth ride.
A candy cane hangs from a branch. Bruiser looks up. Sweet things come to the patient.
Tinsel makes a fine wig. Winnie wears it with confidence.
Puppies in a wicker basket among glass ornaments. Careful, little ones.
lw: The first snow falls, and the shop windows glow.

Winnie and Bruiser walk the small-town street in the falling snow. Their paws leave tiny prints. A Yorkie is small enough to carry and too proud to be carried. Tonight, it walks. The lights are on, and the town is soft.

p: The silky little shadow from Cuba.
s: The Havanese is a cloud with a tail. It floats across the room, curls into your lap, and follows you everywhere you go.

The breed comes from Cuba. Spanish settlers brought small white dogs to the island, and they mixed with local dogs and with Bichon types. Over centuries they became the pets of wealthy Cuban families, and the coat grew long and silky.

The Havanese is the national dog of Cuba. In 1959, when families left the island during the revolution, a few took their dogs along. Those few dogs became the base of the American breed. The AKC recognized it in 1996.
Charles Dickens had one named Timber Doodle. Most Havanese are less famous. They are loved at home and bounce through the house like they own it.
A Havanese is playful, sociable, and clingy. People call it a velcro dog. It does not like to be alone. It does like children, cats, and cookies.
Brush the silky coat, plan for company, and expect to be followed everywhere. A Havanese will be your shadow with a wag.
rc: The little silk dog of Cuba (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Havana, the Cuban capital. Early names included the Havana Silk Dog.
Notable Havanese
Timber Doodle, Charles Dickens’s dog. The breed is also the national dog of Cuba.
Good to Know
Hates being alone. Needs brushing several times a week. Quick to learn tricks.
Coats & Colors
A long, silky, wavy double coat. Cream, chocolate, black, and parti colors.
By the Numbers
Seven to thirteen pounds. Eight and a half to eleven and a half inches tall. Recognized by the AKC in 1996.

p: The Italian guardian that came back from the brink.
s: The Cane Corso is a muscular, quiet guardian with a thoughtful face. It does not bark much. It does not need to.

The breed comes from Italy. Its ancestors are the large molosser war dogs of ancient Rome, which fought beside legions and guarded farms. In the countryside, the Corso drove cattle, hunted boar, and guarded the homestead.
By the mid-1900s, the breed was nearly extinct. A few Italian enthusiasts gathered the last good dogs in the 1970s and rebuilt the line. The AKC recognized the Cane Corso in 2010.
Cane is Italian for dog. Corso probably comes from the Latin cohors, meaning guardian. The name is simple. The dog is a guardian.
At home, a Cane Corso is devoted, calm, and watchful. It is not for beginners. It needs early training, steady leadership, and plenty of exercise.
Give it a job, a fence, and a firm and fair owner. A Corso will protect you, and it will love you quietly.
rc: A Roman guardian reborn in Italy (AKC)
f: Origin of the Name
Cane is Italian for dog. Corso likely comes from the Latin cohors, a guardian.
Notable Cane Corsos
Few are famous by name. The breed itself is a comeback story, from near extinction to the AKC in 2010.
Good to Know
Powerful and strong-willed. Needs early training and socializing. Not for first-time owners.
Coats & Colors
A short, stiff coat in black, gray, fawn, red, or brindle. Often a dark mask.
By the Numbers
Ninety to one hundred twenty pounds. Twenty-three and a half to twenty-seven and a half inches. Recognized by the AKC in 2010.
